"These groups are late and marginal."

Paul's opponents are mid-1st century and Ignatius' early 2nd century; the Seth treatise is 3rd century.

Your opponent says

“Every serious historian accepts the crucifixion.”

Historians accept that Jesus' followers believed he was crucified, and the Quran says it was made to appear so. But "every historian" is not the same as "every early Christian": the records of Paul, Ignatius and Polycarp show Christians who denied or doubted it within living memory.

Paul, Ignatius and Polycarp argued against Christians who denied the crucifixion; Basilides, the Seth treatise and the Mandaeans said Jesus was not crucified; Allison admits some early believers thought he only seemed to die.

s-cross--the-independent-non-christian-w.html: The non-Christian sources cited for the crucifixion (Josephus, Tacitus, Thallus, Mara bar Serapion) are either interpolated, report what Christians believed decades later, or do not mention Jesus at all.

1. P1An independent witness must be early, authentic and not dependent on Christian reports.
  2. P2Josephus' passage on Jesus has been rewritten by Christians; Tacitus wrote 80 years later about what Christians believed; Thallus is lost and never names Jesus; Mara bar Serapion never names Jesus or a crucifixion.
  3. ∴There is no independent, contemporary non-Christian confirmation of the crucifixion; all we have is evidence of what Christians believed, which the Quran grants.

Josephus (the "Testimonium Flavianum", Antiquities 18.3.3, c. 93). As it stands it calls Jesus "the Christ" and says he rose on the third day, which no believing Jew would write. No Christian writer cites it before Eusebius (c. 324), although at least eight earlier fathers quote Josephus. Origen, who knew Josephus well, says twice that Josephus did not believe Jesus was the Christ (Contra Celsum 1.47; Commentary on Matthew 10.17), which contradicts the text we have. Louis Feldman's survey of 87 discussions (1937-1980) found only 13 treating the passage as wholly interpolated; most accepted a partly authentic core. Some scholars (K.A. Olson and others) argue Eusebius composed it. Eusebius titled Praeparatio Evangelica 12.31 "that it will be necessary sometimes to use falsehood as a remedy", in a chapter citing Plato on the "noble lie", and the historian Jacob Burckhardt called him "the first thoroughly dishonest historian of antiquity".

Many scholars do hold that a shorter core of the passage is authentic. Even so, a core saying Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross, written sixty years later in Rome, tells us what was reported, not what happened, and the Quran already grants that it appeared so.

Tacitus (Annals 15.44, c. 116). He says Christus "suffered the extreme penalty under Pontius Pilate". He writes over 80 years later, while explaining who the Christians were, so he is reporting Christian belief or common knowledge about Christians. Bart Ehrman says Tacitus' information "is not particularly helpful" for establishing the historical Jesus.

Others. Thallus' work is lost; we know it through Julius Africanus as quoted by George Syncellus (c. 800), and Thallus apparently only mentioned an eclipse, not Jesus. Mara bar Serapion mentions an unnamed "wise king" of the Jews, says nothing of a crucifixion, and survives in a 7th-century manuscript. Pliny and Suetonius describe Christians, not the event.

"Even sceptics like Ehrman accept the crucifixion."

Ehrman accepts the crucifixion on several grounds, including Paul, multiple Gospels, Josephus and Tacitus, and the embarrassment of a crucified Messiah (a crucified Messiah was embarrassing, so Christians wouldn't invent it). But the crucifixion became the centre of Paul's theology, which shows it was useful, not embarrassing. And scholars such as Rafael Rodríguez and Dale Allison have shown that these criteria are subjective. If all four Gospels proudly report it, it was not something Christians were embarrassed to tell.

"Multiple attestation in the Gospels proves it."

The Gospels depend on each other (Matthew and Luke copy Mark), so they are not independent witnesses, and all reflect the community's belief, which the Quran grants.

Your opponent says

“Are you saying everyone in the first century was wrong?”

I'm saying what the Quran says: it was made to appear so. Every source shows what people believed. None is an eyewitness account by a neutral party. A belief being widespread doesn't tell you whether appearances were deceptive.

Josephus' passage was rewritten by Christians and is unknown before Eusebius; Tacitus writes 80 years later about Christian belief; Thallus and Mara say nothing about Jesus' crucifixion. They show what people believed, which the Quran grants.

s-cross--the-gospel-accounts-of-the-deat.html: On the day, the hour, who carried the cross, what Jesus said, who went to the tomb, what they saw, and where Jesus appeared, the Gospels disagree.

1. P1Eyewitness-based accounts of the central event of a faith should agree on its basic facts.
  2. P2The four Gospels contradict each other on many basic facts of the crucifixion and resurrection.
  3. ∴The accounts are not reliable records of what happened; they are developing traditions, which fits "they are in doubt about it" (4:157).

• The day. In Mark, Jesus eats the Passover meal and is crucified the next day (Mark 14:12; 15:25). In John, he is crucified on "the day of Preparation of the Passover", before the meal (John 19:14).
  • The hour. Mark: "it was the third hour when they crucified him" (15:25). John: at "about the sixth hour" Jesus was still before Pilate (19:14).
  • The cross. Simon of Cyrene carried it (Mark 15:21, Matthew, Luke); Jesus carried it himself (John 19:17). Some scholars think John is countering the tradition that Simon was crucified in his place.
  • The robbers. Both mocked him (Mark 15:32); one rebuked the other and was promised paradise (Luke 23:39-43).
  • The wine. Jesus vowed not to drink wine until the kingdom came (Matt 26:29), but in John he drinks sour wine on the cross (19:29-30).
  • Last words. "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34); "Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit" (Luke 23:46); "It is finished" (John 19:30).
  • At the tomb. One young man (Mark), one angel (Matthew), two men (Luke), two angels (John). The women told no one (Mark 16:8) or told everything to the eleven (Luke 24:9).
  • Where he appeared. In Matthew the disciples are sent to Galilee (28:10, 16). In Luke they are told to stay in Jerusalem (24:49).
  • How long. Luke's Gospel seems to have Jesus ascend on the day of the resurrection (24:50-51), while Acts, by the same author, says forty days (Acts 1:3).
  • Who saw him first. Mary Magdalene (John 20); the two Marys (Matthew 28); Peter, according to Paul's list (1 Cor 15:5), which also says "the Twelve" though Judas was dead and Matthew says "the eleven".
  • Three days and three nights. Jesus said he would be in the earth "three days and three nights" (Matt 12:40), but Friday afternoon to Sunday dawn is at most two nights.

"Different perspectives aren't contradictions. Witnesses always vary in details."

Some can be harmonised with effort, but not all: Jesus cannot be crucified both before and after the Passover meal, both carry and not carry the cross, and the disciples cannot both go to Galilee and stay in Jerusalem. C.K. Barrett said there is no point trying to harmonise the wine passages.

"The core agrees: he died and rose."

The core is what was believed. The Quran agrees that people believed it. The question is whether these accounts are reliable enough to overturn revelation, and their disagreement on basic facts shows they are not.

Your opponent says

“If the Gospels all agreed, you'd say they copied each other; if they differ, you call them contradictions.”

I accept that three of them do copy each other (Matthew and Luke use Mark). The problem is that they copy and still change the facts, for example Matthew changing Mark's "the women said nothing" and John changing the day. That's editing, not independent testimony.

The Gospels disagree on the day and hour of the crucifixion, who carried the cross, the last words, who was at the tomb, whether the women spoke, where Jesus appeared and how long he stayed. Mark 16:8 originally ended with no appearance at all.

s-cross--the-bible-promised-the-righteou.html: Psalms and other scriptures used by Christians for Jesus promise that God would deliver His righteous servant from death, and the NT says Jesus' prayer to be saved from death was heard.

1. P1If God promised to rescue His righteous servant from his enemies, and Jesus prayed to be saved from death and "was heard", the natural conclusion is that God rescued him.
  2. P2Psalm 118, Psalm 91 and the Wisdom of Solomon, all applied to Jesus by Christians, promise rescue, and Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus' prayer to be saved from death was heard.
  3. ∴Christian scripture itself points toward Jesus being saved, as the Quran says.

• Hebrews 5:7: "…and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to Him who was able to save him from death (Greek ek thanatou, which most commentators take to mean out of death by resurrection), and he was heard because of his reverence." If he was heard, he was saved from death.
  • Psalm 118. The NT applies verse 22 ("the stone the builders rejected") to Jesus (Matt 21:42). The same psalm says: "I was pushed hard so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me" (v. 13); "I shall not die, but I shall live… The LORD has disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death" (vv. 17-18).
  • Wisdom of Solomon 2:12-20. The wicked plot against "the righteous man" who "calls himself a child of the Lord", saying: "if the righteous man is God's son, He will help him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries… let us condemn him to a shameful death". Pseudo-Hippolytus (Against the Jews 9) and Augustine (City of God 17.20) apply this passage to Christ. Wisdom 2:12-20 has the wicked expect his death, and Wisdom 3:1-5 says the righteous "seemed to have died" but are in God's hand.
  • Psalm 91. "He will command His angels concerning you… On their hands they will bear you up" (91:11-12), quoted of Jesus by Satan in Matthew 4:6. "Because he holds fast to Me in love, I will deliver him" (91:14).
  • Jesus escaping before. In Luke 4:29-30 the crowd tries to throw him off a cliff "but passing through their midst, he went away"; in John 8:59 "Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple"; "they sought to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come" (John 7:30). And in Gethsemane he says he could call on "twelve legions of angels" (Matt 26:53).
  • Ascension language. Acts 1:11 uses "taken up" (analemphtheis), the language of Elijah's ascension (2 Kgs 2:11 LXX). Enoch and Elijah were taken without dying, and people in Jesus' time identified him with Elijah (Mark 8:28). Vermes discusses this "assumption" model.

إِذْ قَالَ اللَّهُ يَا عِيسَىٰ إِنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا

3:55

"Hebrews 5:7 means he was heard by being resurrected after death."

The verse says God was able "to save him from death", not "out of death after dying". Resurrection after death is not being saved from death.

"The Psalms are about David, not Jesus."

The NT applies them to Jesus. If they are prophecies of Jesus, they promise rescue; if they are not, the NT misuses them. Either way they don't support a crucifixion.

Your opponent says

“Jesus said he must suffer and die.”

Those predictions are widely regarded by scholars as written after the fact (see above), and the disciples acted as if they had never heard them. Meanwhile Hebrews says his own prayer to be saved from death was heard.

Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus' prayer to be saved from death was heard. Psalms 118 and 91 and Wisdom 2, all applied to Jesus by Christians, promise God would deliver him. The ascension language matches Elijah, who was taken up alive.

s-cross--the-shroud-the-swoon-theory-and.html: The physical "evidence" Christians cite for the death and resurrection fails: the Shroud of Turin is a medieval artefact and the Nazareth Inscription is not about Jesus. And when Christians cite sceptical historians, they ignore that the same historians reject the resurrection.

1. P1Physical evidence must be authentic and relevant.
  2. P2The Shroud is dated to 1260-1390 and its first record calls it a painting; the Nazareth Inscription's marble comes from Kos and it never mentions Jesus.
  3. ∴Neither provides evidence for Jesus' death or resurrection.

The Shroud of Turin. Its first documented exhibition was at Lirey in the 1350s; the 1389 memo from Bishop Pierre d'Arcis is the first record claiming it was painted. The memo was addressed to Pope Clement VII and said an earlier bishop had found it "cunningly painted" and that the artist had confessed. In 1988 three laboratories (Arizona, Oxford, Zürich) radiocarbon-dated it to AD 1260-1390. Walter McCrone found iron-oxide and vermilion pigment. Borrini and Garlaschelli (Journal of Forensic Sciences, 2018) found the bloodstain patterns inconsistent with a real body and concluded it was an "artistic or didactic representation" of the 14th century. Andrea Nicolotti has shown no Christian looked for Jesus' burial cloths before the 6th century, and many competing "shrouds" were venerated.

The Nazareth Inscription. A Roman decree against tomb robbing, sometimes linked to the empty tomb. It has no known provenance, never mentions Jesus, and a 2020 isotope study (Harper et al., Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports) traced the marble to Kos and proposed a link with the desecration of the tomb of the tyrant Nikias.

Survival. Some historians (Hugh Schonfield, Barbara Thiering, and others discussed by Allison and Vermes) have argued Jesus survived crucifixion. Josephus records that he saw three acquaintances crucified, had them taken down, and one survived (Life 420-421). Muslims do not need this theory, since the Quran says he was not crucified at all, but it shows that "he died" is not the only historical option.

"The radiocarbon sample came from a medieval repair."

This claim has been examined and rejected by the original laboratories; the sample area was chosen by textile experts, and later statistical reanalyses of the 1988 data have not changed the medieval date, though some found heterogeneity. The 1389 memo independently says it was painted.

Your opponent says

“The Shroud has an image science can't explain.”

Science has explained it well enough: pigment was found, the blood patterns don't fit a body, a 2025 3D study found the image fits a low-relief sculpture better than a body, and the cloth dates to the century when it first appears in history with a bishop calling it a painting.
The Shroud dates to 1260-1390, its first record calls it a painting, and forensic studies find its bloodstains unrealistic. The Nazareth Inscription comes from Kos and never mentions Jesus.

s-cross--mutawaffika-3-55-does-not-mean-.html: The verb tawaffa means "to take fully", and the Quran uses it for sleep. Some early authorities understood 3:55 as Jesus being taken up alive, while others (Wahb, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abbas in one report) said he died briefly first. This answers both Christians and Ahmadis who claim the Quran admits his death.

1. P1A word's meaning is fixed by its use in the same text.
  2. P2The Quran uses tawaffa for both death (2:234; 16:70) and sleep (6:60; 39:42). Early commentators understood 3:55 as being taken alive.
  3. ∴3:55 says Allah took Jesus fully, body and soul, and raised him; it does not say he died.

• Sleep. "It is He who takes you (yatawaffakum) by night" (6:60); "Allah takes (yatawaffa) the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die, in their sleep" (39:42). The Prophet's ﷺ waking supplication thanks Allah "who gave us life after He caused us to die", meaning sleep (Bukhari 6324).
  • Tabari reports the view that tawaffa here means taking him from the earth alive; al-Rabi' said he was raised while asleep; al-Hasan al-Basri reported in a mursal narration that the Prophet ﷺ told the Jews that "Jesus did not die; he will return to you before the Day of Resurrection".
  • Ibn Abbas said Jesus was raised alive through an opening in the roof of the house (Ibn Abi Hatim; graded sound by Ibn Kathir). The report that Ibn Abbas glossed mutawaffika as "I will cause you to die" comes through Ali ibn Abi Talha, who did not meet him, and Ibn Abbas himself placed that death after Jesus' return, since the conjunction "and" (wa) in Arabic does not impose sequence.
  • 5:117 ("when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them") likewise refers to his being taken up.

"Tawaffa usually means death."

Often, when the context is death. Here the context is Allah rescuing Jesus from those who plotted against him (3:54) and raising him (3:55), and 4:157-158 explicitly denies his killing and says Allah raised him. Tawaffa without death is attested in the Quran itself.

Your opponent says

“The Quran says Jesus died (3:55), so it agrees with Christians.”

The Quran says mutawaffika, which it uses for sleep in 6:60 and 39:42, and in 4:157-158 it denies he was killed. And it is Christians who say he died on the cross; the Quran denies that explicitly.
Tawaffa means "take fully" and is used in the Quran for sleep. Tabari, al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas understood 3:55 as Jesus taken up alive, and the "cause you to die" report has a broken chain.

s-jewish-xn--son-of-god-and-father-are-t.html: In the Bible, "son of God" is used for Israel, kings, angels and righteous people. The early sermons in Acts call Jesus God's pais, "servant", which is exactly the Arabic 'Abdullah.

1. P1If "son of God" is applied throughout the Bible to created beings, the title alone cannot prove deity.
  2. P2The Bible calls Israel, David, Adam, angels and peacemakers sons of God, and the earliest preaching in Acts calls Jesus God's servant.
  3. ∴"Son of God" means one close to and obedient to God; it is compatible with Jesus being a human prophet.

• Others called sons of God. Israel: "Israel is My firstborn son" (Exod 4:22). The Davidic king: "You are My son; today I have begotten you" (Ps 2:7). Adam, "the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Angels (Job 38:7). Peacemakers: "they shall be called sons of God" (Matt 5:9). "All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God" (Rom 8:14).
  • Jesus speaks of "my Father and your Father", which some read as sharing his relationship to God and others as distinguishing it: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17).
  • The servant. In Peter's early sermons, Jesus is God's pais: "God glorified His servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13, 26; 4:27, 30). This echoes Isaiah 52:13 in the Greek: "Behold, My servant (pais) will be exalted." Joel Carmichael observed that pais tou theou, "servant of God", is exactly the Arabic 'Abdullah. The Quran's first words from the infant Jesus are "I am the servant of Allah" (19:30).
  • The growth of "Father". Jesus calls God "Father" about 4 times in Mark, about 15-17 in Luke, about 40-45 in Matthew and over 100 in John. The later the Gospel, the more the Father-Son language, a sign of developing theology.
  • Muslim scholars on the term. Ibn Taymiyya (al-Jawab al-Sahih) explained that in the earlier scriptures "father" meant the merciful Lord who nurtures, and "son" meant a beloved servant, so the words were not originally blasphemous. The Quran forbids them now because they were taken literally, just as God told Israel to stop calling Him "Baali" ("my master") because of its pagan associations (Hosea 2:16).

قَالَ إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ وَجَعَلَنِي نَبِيًّا

19:30

"Jesus is the Son, monogenes, unique."

Monogenes means "one of a kind" and is used of Isaac (Heb 11:17), who was not Abraham's only son. Uniqueness of status is not deity: David was uniquely "begotten" as king (Ps 2:7), and Israel was uniquely God's "firstborn".

"The Jews wanted to kill him for calling God his Father (John 5:18)."

That is the opponents' interpretation; Jesus' reply is "the Son can do nothing of himself" (5:19). And when accused of making himself God (John 10:33), he answers that Scripture calls humans "gods" (10:34-36).

Your opponent says

“If "Son of God" just means "servant", why does the Quran attack it so strongly (19:88-92)?”

Because by the Quran's time it was used literally, to mean a begotten divine being. The Quran rejects that meaning, as God rejected "Baali" in Hosea 2:16 once it carried pagan meaning. The Quran keeps the original idea under its proper name: Jesus is 'Abdullah.

Israel, David, Adam, angels and peacemakers are all "sons of God" in the Bible. Peter's early sermons call Jesus God's pais, his servant, which is 'Abdullah. The Father-Son language multiplies in the later Gospels.

s-jewish-xn--the-original-jerusalem-chur.html: The church led by James in Jerusalem, and its heirs the Ebionites (and, on some readings, the Nazarenes) held that Jesus was a human Messiah and prophet, kept the Law and rejected Paul. Some scholars regard Jewish-Christian groups as continuing the Jerusalem church, but this is disputed.

1. P1The community founded by Jesus' own family and disciples is the best guide to what Jesus taught.
  2. P2That community, led by James, kept the Law, and its descendants (Nazarenes and Ebionites) held Jesus to be a human prophet-Messiah and rejected Paul.
  3. ∴The original followers of Jesus held beliefs much closer to Islam than to later Christianity.

• They were the majority at first. Alan Segal describes Jewish Christians as a "comfortable majority" of the movement in the first generation.
  • James led them. Eusebius (Church History 2.1) and Hegesippus name James the Just as the first leader of the Jerusalem church. In the Gospel of Thomas (saying 12) Jesus tells the disciples: "go to James the Just".
  • Justin Martyr (c. 150) admits some "of our race" (Christians of Jewish origin) held Jesus to be "a man of men" who became Christ by God's election (Dialogue 48).
  • Epiphanius says the Nazarenes descended from the Jerusalem church that fled to Pella before 70 CE (Panarion 29). Kegan Zarley argues that a Nazarene rejection of Jesus' deity is strong evidence that the apostolic Jerusalem church held the same view.
  • The Ebionites (from Hebrew evyonim, "the poor", cf. Gal 2:10) held Jesus to be a human being, the prophet and Messiah. Origen says there were "two kinds" of Ebionites, one of which accepted the virgin birth (Contra Celsum 5.61), just as Islam does. They kept circumcision, the Sabbath and the Law; rejected animal sacrifice; revered James; regarded Paul as an apostate; and held that false passages had entered the Hebrew Bible (H.J. Schoeps). Jerome says John's Gospel was written against them, which shows how early they were.
  • Petri Luomanen finds that the Ebionites described by Irenaeus match the profile of the early Jerusalem church. Schoeps concluded that Jewish Christianity "disappeared within the church, but was preserved in Islam".

"The Ebionites were a late heretical sect."

Irenaeus already knows them around 180, and their link to the Jerusalem church is attested by Epiphanius. They were called heretics by the Gentile church that replaced them, which is what we would expect if the Gentile church had changed the message.

"Ebionites denied the virgin birth, which Islam affirms."

Only some did; Origen and Eusebius (Church History 3.27) describe a group that affirmed it. Islam doesn't need to agree with every Ebionite; the point is that the original community held Jesus to be a human prophet.

Your opponent says

“The New Testament is the apostolic record, and it doesn't say what the Ebionites said.”

Most of the New Testament is by Paul or from churches Paul founded. The only letter from the Jerusalem church, James, says justification is by works and never calls Jesus God. Acts 21 shows James' community "zealous for the Law" and suspicious of Paul.

Jesus' first followers, led by his brother James, kept the Law and saw him as a human Messiah. Their heirs, the Nazarenes and Ebionites, rejected Paul and Jesus' deity, and Schoeps concluded their faith survived in Islam.

s-jewish-xn--jesus-practised-islam-submi.html: Jesus prayed by prostrating, fasted, affirmed the Shema, kept the Law and called people to obey God, exactly the practice the Quran ascribes to every prophet.

1. P1Islam means submission to the one God through prayer, fasting, obedience to His law and belief in His messengers.
  2. P2The Gospels show Jesus prostrating in prayer, fasting, affirming the Shema, upholding the Law and teaching obedience to God's will.
  3. ∴Jesus' religion was Islam in its essential sense, as the Quran states (3:52; 5:111).

• Prostration. "He fell on his face and prayed" (Matt 26:39), the same posture as the Muslim sujud.
  • Fasting. Jesus fasted forty days (Matt 4:2) and taught his disciples how to fast (Matt 6:16-18).
  • The Shema. "The first commandment is: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29).
  • The Law. "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfil… until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota… will pass from the Law" (Matt 5:17-18). "If you would enter life, keep the commandments" (Matt 19:17).
  • Submission. "Not my will, but Yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). "My food is to do the will of Him who sent me" (John 4:34).
  • Greeting. "Peace be with you" (John 20:19), the Aramaic shlama 'alaykhon, the Arabic as-salamu 'alaykum.
  • James' letter echoes the Sermon on the Mount repeatedly (Matt 5:3 and James 2:5; Matt 5:34-37 and James 5:12), and James calls himself "a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1).

قَالَ الْحَوَارِيُّونَ نَحْنُ أَنصَارُ اللَّهِ آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَاشْهَدْ بِأَنَّا مُسْلِمُونَ

3:52

"Jesus fulfilled the Law so Christians don't have to keep it."

"Fulfil" in Matthew 5:17 is immediately explained by verses 18-19: not the smallest letter will pass away, and whoever relaxes the least commandment will be least in the kingdom. That is the opposite of abolition.

Your opponent says

“Jesus didn't pray five times a day or fast Ramadan, so he wasn't a Muslim.”

The specific forms of law differ between prophets (5:48), but the religion is one: worship the one God and obey His messenger. Jesus prostrated, fasted, kept his Law and affirmed God's oneness, which is islam.
Jesus prostrated, fasted, recited the Shema, upheld every letter of the Law, and submitted to God's will. His disciples in the Quran say "bear witness that we are Muslims" (3:52).

s-jewish-xn--quran-61-14-who-were-the-be.html: Christians claim 61:14 endorses Trinitarian Christianity as the "dominant" group. In context, the believers who prevailed are those who believed in Jesus as God's messenger, and their vindication came through the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

1. P1The Quran praises only belief in Jesus as a servant and messenger of God (4:171; 5:72-75).
  2. P261:14 says one group of the Children of Israel believed in Jesus and another disbelieved, and "We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant".
  3. ∴The supported group must be those who believed what the Quran teaches about Jesus, not Trinitarians, whom the Quran calls disbelievers (5:73).

The surah's context is Moses and Jesus being rejected (61:5-6), then the promise that Allah will make His religion prevail over all religions (61:9, li-yuzhirahu), which commentators apply to Islam. The same root (z-h-r) appears in 61:14 (zahirin, "dominant").

Classical commentators such as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Muqatil explain that the believers in Jesus became dominant when Muhammad ﷺ came and confirmed their position: the truth about Jesus they held was vindicated over the views of their opponents. The Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions, a Jewish-Christian text, has a similar idea: "the truth everywhere prevailed; we who were few became far more". And Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, fled to Pella before Jerusalem's destruction in 70, so it was rescued while its enemies were punished (Church History 3.5).

فَآمَنَت طَّائِفَةٌ مِّن بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ وَكَفَرَت طَّائِفَةٌ ۖ فَأَيَّدْنَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا عَلَىٰ عَدُوِّهِمْ فَأَصْبَحُوا ظَاهِرِينَ

61:14

"Historically, the Trinitarians are the ones who became dominant."

The Quran does not call Trinitarians "those who believed"; it calls their belief disbelief (5:73). The verse's "believers" are defined by the Quran's own standard, and their final vindication is the spread of Islam's account of Jesus.

Your opponent says

“The Quran says Jesus' followers became dominant, and Trinitarian Christians are the ones who did. So the Quran endorses them.”

That reads "believers" in a way the Quran itself rejects (5:72-73). In the Quran, believers in Jesus are those who said "we are Muslims" (3:52). Their position prevailed through the final messenger, as 61:9 promises.
61:14's "believers" are those who believed in Jesus as the Quran describes him; the Quran calls Trinitarian belief disbelief. Their vindication came through Islam, as the surah promises in 61:9.

s-paul--paul-s-authority-rests-on-a-priv.html: Paul says he received his gospel from no human being, and the Jerusalem leaders (James and Peter) and their followers opposed him. Later Jewish-Christian texts (the Pseudo-Clementines, 3rd-4th century in their final form) have Peter denounce "the man who is my enemy", which many scholars read as an allusion to Paul.

1. P1A claim to speak for Jesus is credible when it is confirmed by those Jesus himself taught.
  2. P2Paul says his gospel came by private revelation, not from the apostles (Gal 1:11-12), he publicly opposed Peter, he says rivals preached "another Jesus", and James' community demanded he prove he kept the Law (Acts 21).
  3. ∴Paul's version of the message was not the apostles' version and has no independent confirmation from Jesus' own disciples.

• Self-certified. "…the gospel that was preached by me is not man's gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ" (Gal 1:11-12). He did not go to the apostles for three years after his conversion (Gal 1:17-18).
  • The vision itself is unstable. In Acts 9:7 his companions "heard the voice but saw no one"; in Acts 22:9 they "saw the light but did not hear the voice". In Acts 26 the commission comes directly from Jesus; in Acts 9 and 22 it comes later through Ananias.
  • Conflict with Peter and James. "When Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face" because "certain men came from James" and Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles (Gal 2:11-12). Paul downplays the status of the Jerusalem leaders as "those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)" (Gal 2:6).
  • "Another Jesus". Paul says rival preachers came to Corinth with "another Jesus" and "a different gospel", and calls them "super-apostles" (2 Cor 11:4-5), and later "false apostles" (11:13). James Tabor argues these were envoys of James and Peter.
  • James' demand. When Paul reached Jerusalem, James told him thousands of believers were "all zealous for the Law" and had heard Paul taught Jews to abandon Moses; he advised Paul to join four men under a vow and pay their expenses, to show that Paul himself lived in observance of the Law (Acts 21:18-26).
  • "The enemy". In the Pseudo-Clementine writings, Peter complains of "the lawless and trifling preaching of the man who is my enemy", and warns believers to accept no teacher who does not bring a testimonial from James. Bishop Westcott acknowledged that "no doubt St Paul is referred to as 'the enemy'". The Ebionites rejected Paul as an apostate.

"Galatians 2:9 says James, Peter and John gave Paul the right hand of fellowship."

They agreed to a division of labour (Paul to the Gentiles, they to the Jews), yet the very next verses describe the Antioch clash. And Acts 21 shows James' community still suspicious years later.

"Peter calls Paul's letters scripture (2 Pet 3:16)."

2 Peter is widely regarded by scholars as pseudonymous, written decades after Peter's death, and it is among the books whose canonicity was disputed longest (see Corruption of the Bible). It even concedes that Paul's letters contain things "hard to understand".

Your opponent says

“Paul was accepted by the church, so his authority is settled.”

He was accepted by the Gentile church he himself founded. The Jerusalem church of Jesus' family opposed him, and their heirs called him "the enemy". Acceptance by his own converts can't validate him.
Paul's gospel came by private vision, he opposed Peter to his face, he said rivals preached "another Jesus", James made him prove he kept the Law, and Jewish-Christian texts call him "the enemy".

s-paul--paul-contradicted-jesus-and-the-.html: Jesus said not one letter of the Law would pass away; the Torah calls circumcision an everlasting covenant and the Psalmist calls the Law perfect. Paul called the Law a curse and a "ministry of death", declared circumcision worthless, and allowed food offered to idols.

1. P1A messenger of the God who gave the Law cannot overturn it without a clear, authenticated command from God.
  2. P2Paul overturned the Law's covenant sign, its food laws and the apostolic decree, and reinterpreted its blessings as curses, with no authorisation from Jesus' teaching.
  3. ∴Paul's teaching on the Law contradicts both the Torah and Jesus.

• Jesus. "Not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom" (Matt 5:18-19).
  • Circumcision. God: "My covenant shall be in your flesh an everlasting covenant" (Gen 17:13); no uncircumcised foreigner may enter the sanctuary (Ezek 44:9). Paul: "if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you" (Gal 5:2); he calls its advocates "dogs… those who mutilate the flesh" (Phil 3:2).
  • The Law's value. "The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul" (Ps 19:7); "it will be righteousness for us if we are careful to do all this commandment" (Deut 6:25). Paul: the Law is a "ministry of death" (2 Cor 3:7) and a "yoke of slavery" (Gal 5:1). In Galatians 3:10 he quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 ("cursed is everyone who does not keep the Law") to prove that everyone who relies on the Law is cursed, turning a warning against neglecting the Law into a warning against keeping it.
  • Idol meat. The Jerusalem council told Gentile believers to "abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols" (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). The risen Jesus condemns churches that eat it (Rev 2:14, 20), and the Didache (6.3) says to "keep strictly from food offered to idols, for it is the worship of dead gods". Paul says "eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question" (1 Cor 10:25) and treats idol meat as a matter of conscience (1 Cor 8). C.K. Barrett notes Paul never mentions the apostolic decree.
  • Mark's gloss. Mark, whom tradition identifies with Paul's companion John Mark (Col 4:10; Phlm 24), adds "thus he declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Matthew, copying Mark, leaves the comment out.

وَمُصَدِّقًا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ وَلِأُحِلَّ لَكُم بَعْضَ الَّذِي حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ

3:50

"Jesus fulfilled the Law, so Paul is applying that."

Matthew 5:18-19 explains "fulfil": the commandments stay in force. Jesus never told his disciples circumcision or food laws were abolished; if he had, the Jerusalem church would not have argued about it for decades (Acts 15; Gal 2).

"Peter's vision in Acts 10 abolished food laws."

Peter himself interprets the vision as being about people, not food: "God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean" (Acts 10:28).

Your opponent says

“Islam also changed the Law of Moses, so why can't Paul?”

The Quran says Jesus made lawful some things that had been forbidden (3:50), by God's authority, and it brought a new revelation with proof. Paul claimed no new scripture from God; he reinterpreted the existing one against its plain meaning and against the apostles who knew Jesus.

Jesus said not a dot of the Law would pass; the Torah calls circumcision everlasting and the Law perfect. Paul called the Law death and slavery, circumcision worthless, and permitted idol meat that the apostles and Revelation forbid.

s-paul--paul-s-methods-all-things-to-all.html: Paul describes himself adapting his practice to his audience, and Acts shows him doing things he condemned in his letters. That makes his teaching hard to treat as consistent revelation.

Christians will reply that Romans 3:7 ("if through my lie God's truth abounds…") is a hypothetical objection Paul is answering, not a confession. That is correct, so don't use Romans 3:7 as a quote of Paul lying. The stronger evidence is 1 Corinthians 9 and his conduct in Acts.

1. P1A messenger of God delivers the same message to all audiences.
  2. P2Paul says he became "as a Jew to the Jews… as one outside the law to those outside the law… all things to all people" (1 Cor 9:20-22), and his conduct varies accordingly.
  3. ∴Paul's teaching was strategically adapted, which undermines treating his letters as a fixed revelation.

• All things to all people. 1 Corinthians 9:20-22.
  • Timothy. Despite saying circumcision makes Christ of no advantage (Gal 5:2), Paul circumcised Timothy "because of the Jews in those places" (Acts 16:3).
  • The Temple vow. He paid for a Nazirite vow in the Temple to show Jewish believers he kept the Law (Acts 21:24-26), while his letters call the Law slavery.
  • Dividing the council. At his trial, seeing Pharisees and Sadducees present, he declared "I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial", setting them against each other (Acts 23:6-10).
  • Sin. The Pastoral letter 1 Timothy has him call himself the foremost of sinners (1:15), and Romans 7:14-24 is read by some as his own struggle (Rom 7:14-24), yet he condemns the Corinthians harshly. Jesus' rule: "a good tree cannot bear bad fruit" (Matt 7:18).

"Being 'all things to all people' means cultural sensitivity, not changing doctrine."

Circumcising Timothy while teaching that circumcision cuts you off from Christ is not just culture; it is acting against his own doctrine for strategic reasons.

Your opponent says

“Paul was a sincere man who died for his faith.”

Sincerity and courage don't make someone a prophet. The question is whether his message matches Jesus' and the Torah's, and his own letters show he adapted it to his audience and contradicted the apostles.

Paul says he became all things to all people, circumcised Timothy after calling circumcision worthless, performed a Temple vow to appear Law-observant, and set his judges against each other. His teaching was strategic, not fixed.

s-paul--paul-and-jesus-predicted-the-end.html: Paul wrote as though he might be alive at Jesus' return, and the Gospels have Jesus promise it within his listeners' lifetime. It did not happen, which by the Torah's test (Deut 18:22) marks a false prophecy.

1. P1"When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the word does not come to pass, that is a word the LORD has not spoken" (Deut 18:22).
  2. P2Paul and the Gospels predict Jesus' return within the lifetime of their hearers.
  3. ∴These predictions were not from God; at least, they show that the NT authors' message was not preserved as divine prophecy.

• Paul. "We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord… will be caught up together with them in the clouds" (1 Thess 4:15-17). "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed" (1 Cor 15:51). "The appointed time has grown very short… the present form of this world is passing away", so the unmarried should stay unmarried (1 Cor 7:29-31). Scholars such as C.K. Barrett and Victor Furnish trace a declining sense of imminence through his letters.
  • The Gospels. "There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" (Matt 16:28). "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matt 24:34). "You will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes" (Matt 10:23). To Caiaphas: "you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds" (Matt 26:64).
  • Revelation. "Behold, I am coming soon (tachu)" (Rev 22:12).
  • The patch. 2 Peter, written late, answers "scoffers" who ask "where is the promise of his coming?" by saying that "with the Lord one day is as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:3-8). It concedes the problem existed.
  • C.S. Lewis called Matthew 24:34 "certainly the most embarrassing verse in the Bible", though he went on to argue that Jesus' admission of ignorance in Matthew 24:36 explains it (The World's Last Night).

"'This generation' means the generation that sees the signs, or the Jewish race."

In Matthew, "this generation" always means Jesus' contemporaries (11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). And Matthew 16:28 and 26:64 use "some standing here" and "you", which leave no room for a future generation.

"'Coming in his kingdom' was the Transfiguration or Pentecost."

Then why did Paul expect to be alive at the coming in the clouds, and why did 2 Peter need to answer scoffers?

Your opponent says

“The Quran also says the Hour is near (54:1).”

The Quran never says it will come within a generation or that the listeners will be alive to see it; it says its time is known only to Allah (7:187), and "near" is relative to the age of creation. Jesus in Matthew names his hearers and their generation.

Paul expected to be alive at the return, and the Gospels have Jesus promise it to "some standing here" and "this generation". 2 Peter had to answer scoffers, and C.S. Lewis called Matthew 24:34 the Bible's most embarrassing verse.

s-paul--paul-s-christ-owes-much-to-greek.html: Paul quotes pagan poets, uses language from Greek religion, and was himself taken for a god by pagans. Even so, he consistently makes Christ subordinate to the Father, so he cannot be used for the later Trinity.

1. P1A teaching that borrows language from pagan religion invites the suspicion that it reshaped Jesus in pagan terms.
  2. P2Paul quotes Aratus' line about Zeus, uses the phrase "kick against the goads" from Euripides' play about Dionysus, and describes Christ's incarnation in language pagans used for gods descending.
  3. P3But Paul still says God is the Father, Christ is subjected to Him, and the head of Christ is God.
  4. ∴Paul's Christ is a Hellenised exalted figure, but even Paul does not teach that he is the one God.

Pagan language.

  • "In Him we live and move and have our being… for we are indeed His offspring" (Acts 17:28) quotes Aratus' Phaenomena ("we are also his offspring", echoed in Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus); "in him we live and move" is traced to Epimenides, both written about Zeus.
  • "It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (Acts 26:14), in Jesus' voice, is a Greek proverb found in Euripides' Bacchae (794-795), where Dionysus says it to his persecutor, and also in Aeschylus and Pindar.
  • At Lystra the crowd shouted "the gods have come down to us in the likeness of men" (Acts 14:11), similar in wording to "being made in the likeness of men" (Philippians 2:7), though many scholars read that hymn against Jewish backgrounds. At Malta the islanders said Paul himself was a god (Acts 28:6).
  • Scholars such as Thomas Wilson describe Paul's Christology as a fusion of the Jewish Messiah with the Hellenistic dying-and-rising divine saviour.

Still subordinate.

  • "For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things" (1 Cor 8:6).
  • "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to Him who put all things under him, that God may be all in all" (1 Cor 15:28).
  • "The head of Christ is God" (1 Cor 11:3).
  • In Galatians 2:20 many early manuscripts (P46, B, D, F, G) read "faith in God and Christ" rather than "the Son of God", a change Ehrman treats as orthodox corruption.

"Paul was evangelising Greeks in their own terms; that's not syncretism."

Quoting a line about Zeus to describe the God of Abraham blurs the difference; and the Quran rejects divine sonship: "He neither begets nor is begotten" (112:3).

Your opponent says

“1 Corinthians 8:6 puts Jesus inside the Shema, so Paul believed Jesus was God.”

Paul divides the Shema: "one God, the Father", and "one Lord, Jesus Christ". God is the Father alone; Jesus is the Lord "through whom". And 15:28 says the Son will be subjected to God so that "God may be all in all". That is subordination.

Paul quotes a poem about Zeus, uses a Dionysus proverb, and was himself taken for a god. Yet even Paul says there is "one God, the Father", that the Son will be subjected to Him, and that the head of Christ is God.

s-paul--beware-of-false-prophets-ravenou.html: Jesus warned of "ravenous wolves" who would do miracles in his name but practise lawlessness. Genesis calls Benjamin, Paul's tribe, "a ravenous wolf", and the warning fits Paul's teaching against the Law.
This is a typological argument. It is suggestive, not a proof; present it as a reading Christians themselves made of Genesis 49:27, not as a definitive identification.

• Jesus: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognise them by their fruits" (Matt 7:15-16). "Many will say to me, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?' Then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness (anomia)'" (7:22-23).
  • Jacob's blessing: "Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil" (Gen 49:27). Paul was "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1; Phil 3:5). Christian fathers including Hippolytus, Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.1), Jerome (Letter 60) and Augustine applied Genesis 49:27 to Paul, as persecutor in the morning and teacher in the evening.
  • Ezekiel's officials are "like wolves tearing the prey" (22:27), and his priests "do violence to My law" and "make no distinction between the holy and the common, clean and unclean" (22:26), disregard the Sabbaths and announce "thus says the Lord God" when the LORD has not spoken.
  • Paul performed miracles and exorcisms in Jesus' name (Acts 16; 19) and taught freedom from the Law.
  • Jesus also said the kingdom would be taken away and given "to a nation producing its fruits" (Matt 21:43), which Muslims apply to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his community.

"The fathers applied Genesis 49:27 to Paul positively."

Yes, but the text's word is "ravenous wolf", and Jesus uses the same image for false prophets. The fathers' identification is what makes the connection; the conclusion depends on whether Paul's teaching is "lawlessness", which the previous arguments address.

Your opponent says

“You're twisting a blessing on Benjamin into a curse on Paul.”

I'm pointing out that the church fathers themselves identified Paul with the Benjamin wolf, and that Jesus' warning describes miracle-workers in his name who practise lawlessness. Whether Paul fits depends on his teaching about the Law, which contradicted Jesus.
Jesus warned of ravenous wolves who work miracles in his name but practise lawlessness; Benjamin, Paul's tribe, is "a ravenous wolf" (Gen 49:27), and several fathers applied that verse to Paul.

s-corruption--the-gospels-are-anonymous-.html: None of the Gospels names its author; the names are first attested for all four Gospels around 180 CE; and most critical scholars hold that none is the work of an eyewitness.

1. P1A text's authority as testimony depends on knowing who wrote it and whether they witnessed the events.
  2. P2The four Gospels are anonymous, their traditional names are first attested for all four around 180 (Irenaeus). Papias (c. 110-130, preserved only in Eusebius) speaks of a Mark who wrote down Peter's teaching “not in order” and a Matthew who compiled the sayings in the Hebrew dialect, but those descriptions do not fit our Mark and our Greek Matthew well, and whether he means them is disputed, so he does not settle the names. The Gospels were written 40-70 years after Jesus in Greek by authors who copy each other and make errors about Palestine.
  3. ∴The Gospels are not eyewitness testimony and cannot be treated as the Injil revealed to Jesus.

• Anonymous. No Gospel names its author in the text. The earliest Christian writers quote "the Gospel" without names (the Didache calls it "the Gospel of our Lord"). Irenaeus, around 180, is the first to name all four (Against Heresies 3.1.1). James Tabor: "All four Gospels are anonymous… names were assigned later by tradition."
  • Not eyewitnesses. The New Oxford Annotated Bible dates them roughly 40 to 70 years after the events. They are not eyewitness accounts. Richard Bauckham, who argues for eyewitness sources, acknowledges that his thesis challenges the form-critical consensus that the Gospel traditions circulated anonymously.
  • Matthew copies Mark. Papias said Matthew compiled "the sayings" (logia) in Hebrew, but our Greek Matthew reproduces most of Mark's content (roughly 80-90%) and about half of its exact wording. An apostle who saw the events would not need to copy a non-apostle's account.
  • Mark's geography. Mark has Jesus go from Tyre "through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the region of the Decapolis" (Mark 7:31), a route like going from London to Paris via Edinburgh. This suggests an author unfamiliar with Palestine.
  • John. Ancient tradition gave at least four different authors. Papias distinguished John the apostle from "John the Elder", and Eusebius noted two tombs of "John" in Ephesus (Church History 3.39). The Alogi (Epiphanius, Panarion 51) attributed John's Gospel and Revelation to Cerinthus, and Gaius of Rome attributed Revelation to him (Eusebius 3.28.2). The final form is usually dated around 90-110.
  • Unreliable oral tradition. Irenaeus claimed, on the authority of "the elders" who knew John, that Jesus lived to nearly fifty (Against Heresies 2.22.5). If the elders' oral tradition could get that wrong, it is no guarantee for the Gospel names.
  • Other books. Origen says of Hebrews: "who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows" (Eusebius, Church History 6.25). Most scholars regard 2 Peter and the Pastoral letters (1-2 Timothy, Titus) as written in the names of apostles who did not write them. Acts is dated by some scholars (Pervo, Mack) into the 2nd century.

فَوَيْلٌ لِّلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ الْكِتَابَ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ هَٰذَا مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ

2:79

"Anonymous doesn't mean unreliable; many ancient histories are anonymous."

For history, perhaps. For scripture that claims divine authority, we need to know it came from a prophet or witness. Muslims know the Quran came through the Prophet ﷺ by mass transmission; Christians do not know who wrote the Gospels.

"The early church unanimously attributed them."

The attributions are unanimous only from Irenaeus on, a century after Jesus. Before that, writers quote Gospel material without names, and later disputes over John's authorship show the "unanimity" was not complete.

Your opponent says

“The Quran is also "anonymous": it doesn't name its human author.”

The Quran claims to be God's speech, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, and its transmission from him is mass-attested, with Companion codices and manuscripts within decades. The Gospels claim to be accounts by people about Jesus, so who they were matters, and we don't know.

The Gospels name no authors; Irenaeus first named them around 180; Matthew copies Mark; Mark errs on Palestinian geography; and scholars from Tabor to the Oxford Annotated Bible agree they are not eyewitness accounts.

s-corruption--the-church-fathers-themsel.html: Celsus, Origen, Dionysius of Corinth and Jerome all complained, in the first four centuries, that Christian scriptures were being altered by scribes, sometimes deliberately.

1. P1If those who copied and used the texts in the early centuries testify that they were being changed, the claim of perfect preservation fails.
  2. P2Origen, Jerome and others complain of deliberate additions and deletions, and Jerome says there were "almost as many forms of text as copies" of the Latin Gospels.
  3. ∴The New Testament text was not preserved unchanged; early Christians themselves say so.

• Celsus (c. 175), quoted by Origen: some believers "alter the original text of the gospel three or four or several times over, and change its character to enable them to deny difficulties" (Contra Celsum 2.27). Origen does not deny it; he says it was done by heretics.
  • Origen himself: "the differences among the manuscripts have become great, either through the negligence of some copyists or through the perverse audacity of others; they either neglect to check over what they have transcribed, or in the process of checking they make additions or deletions as they please" (Commentary on Matthew 15.14).
  • Dionysius of Corinth (c. 170) complained that his own letters had been altered and added: "no wonder some have attempted to adulterate the Lord's writings" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23).
  • Jerome (383), commissioned by Pope Damasus to revise the Latin Bible: there are "almost as many forms of text as there are copies", corrupted by inaccurate translators, "the blundering alterations of confident but ignorant critics", and copyists "more asleep than awake" (Preface to the Gospels). Bruce Metzger notes that Jerome catalogues the kinds of scribal error, including conscious emendation.
  • A scribe's own complaint. In Codex Vaticanus, at Hebrews 1:3, a later corrector changed a word, and another scribe wrote in the margin: "Fool and knave! Leave the old reading, don't change it!"
  • The Old Testament too. Justin Martyr accused the Jews of removing passages from Jeremiah and the Psalms (Dialogue 71-73), and quotes a "Jeremiah" text found in no manuscript. Chrysostom says Jews burned books and copies perished. Cardinal Bellarmine listed Justin, Origen, Eusebius and Chrysostom as holding that Jews had corrupted the Old Testament.
  • Helmut Koester: the text-types we can reconstruct go back only to around 200, and "substantial revisions" happened during the first hundred years.

"They're talking about heretics' copies, which were caught."

Origen speaks of "copyists" generally, and Jerome speaks of the copies in the church's own hands. If corruption was widespread enough for Jerome to see as many texts as copies, we cannot assume every change was caught, especially in the first century where we have almost no manuscripts.

"Textual criticism lets us recover the original."

It lets us recover the text as of the 2nd-3rd centuries, the earliest substantial manuscripts. Koester's point is that the most important changes would have happened before then.

Your opponent says

“You're quoting Christians who loved the Bible. They were complaining about scribes, not saying the Bible is false.”

Exactly: they loved the Bible and still testified that copyists added and deleted "as they please". That is the Quran's charge (2:79; 4:46). Their love makes the testimony more credible, not less.

Celsus, Origen, Dionysius of Corinth and Jerome all complained that texts were being altered; Jerome said there were almost as many forms of text as copies; a Vaticanus scribe wrote "Fool and knave, leave the old reading!"

s-corruption--major-passages-were-added-.html: The longer ending of Mark, the story of the adulteress, the Trinitarian baptism formula, the Johannine Comma and several smaller changes are later additions or alterations, and many of them carry central doctrines.

1. P1A passage absent from the earliest manuscripts and the earliest fathers, and inconsistent with its context, is a later addition.
  2. P2Mark 16:9-20, John 7:53-8:11 and 1 John 5:7 meet these tests clearly; Matthew 28:19 is textually secure in every Greek manuscript, but its formula is in tension with Acts and with Eusebius' shorter quotations.
  3. ∴Important passages of the New Testament, including texts on the resurrection appearances, forgiveness, and the Trinity, were added after the books were written.

Mark 16:9-20. Absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest complete manuscripts. Eusebius and Jerome say almost all Greek copies of their time lacked it, and it is not in the Eusebian canon tables. Its style differs; it re-introduces Mary Magdalene as if she had not been mentioned (taking a detail from Luke 8:2); and it ignores Mark's own promise of a meeting in Galilee (14:28; 16:7). Scholars broadly agree it is not original to Mark and was added in the 2nd century or earlier (Irenaeus quotes it c. 180).

John 7:53-8:11 (the woman caught in adultery). Absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and the early Syriac and Coptic versions; Origen and Chrysostom skip it in their commentaries; later manuscripts place it in different spots (even in Luke). Metzger: "the evidence for the non-Johannine origin of the pericope of the adulteress is overwhelming".

Matthew 28:19 ("baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"). In Acts, the apostles baptise only "in the name of Jesus" (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5), which is strange if Jesus had commanded the triadic formula. Eusebius quotes the verse many times before Nicaea in a short form: "Go and make disciples of all nations in my name". The medieval (14th-century) Hebrew Matthew in Shem Tob's Even Bohan lacks the formula, though its antiquity is debated. Geza Vermes argues the formula is "unheard of anywhere in the NT" apart from Matthew 28:19 itself and the Didache (7.1), and is of late Gentile origin. It also conflicts with Jesus' instruction "go nowhere among the Gentiles" (Matt 10:5-6) and "I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel" (15:24).

1 John 5:7. "The Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one" appears in no Greek manuscript before the late Middle Ages and was not quoted by any Greek father in the Trinitarian debates, where it would have been decisive. It entered the Greek printed text through Erasmus' third edition (1522).

Smaller theological changes.

  • Luke 23:32: the earliest manuscripts read "other criminals, two, were led away with him" (heteroi kakourgoi duo), which could imply Jesus was a criminal; later scribes reordered it to "two others, criminals".
  • John 7:8: Jesus says "I am not going up to this feast", then goes (7:10). Scribes changed it to "not yet" (already found in P66 and P75, earlier than Porphyry's criticism), while Epiphanius, Jerome and others knew the reading "not".
  • Matthew 24:36: "nor the Son" deleted (see Jesus is not God).
  • Mark 1:1: "the Son of God" is missing from the first hand of Sinaiticus.

"No doctrine depends on these passages."

The longer ending of Mark is the only resurrection appearance in Mark; the Comma was the only explicit Trinity verse; Matthew 28:19 is the only Trinitarian baptism command. That these are the passages under suspicion is exactly the point: the doctrines grew, and texts were added to match.

"Matthew 28:19 is in every Greek manuscript."

Our Greek manuscripts of Matthew 28 begin in the 4th century. Eusebius' pre-Nicene quotations and the practice in Acts are evidence of an earlier form. You can concede the textual question is debated while pointing out the tension with Acts and Matthew 10:5-6.

Your opponent says

“If the Bible was corrupted, why do Christians still have the original words in footnotes?”

Because scholars have caught some of the later additions by comparing manuscripts. But the earliest manuscripts are themselves 2nd-4th century copies, so changes made in the first century, before our evidence starts, can't be detected the same way.

Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 are absent from the oldest manuscripts; 1 John 5:7 is a medieval addition; Matthew 28:19's formula clashes with Acts and with Eusebius' quotations; and scribes altered Luke 23:32, John 7:8 and Matthew 24:36 for theological reasons.

s-corruption--the-hebrew-bible-shows-del.html: Emanuel Tov, the leading textual critic of the Hebrew Bible, accepts that scribes made theological alterations, and the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve readings that the standard Hebrew text changed.

1. P1If the standard Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text) contains deliberate changes, it is not the original revelation unchanged.
  2. P2Tov documents theological alterations accepted by most scholars, the Masoretic Text of Samuel is "frequently corrupt", and older editions of Jeremiah and Joshua survive in shorter forms.
  3. ∴The Hebrew Bible was edited and altered, which supports the Muslim position that the earlier scriptures were not preserved perfectly.

• Theological alterations. Tov writes that "the existence of theological changes… is accepted by most scholars".
  • Deuteronomy 32:8. The Masoretic Text says God divided the nations "according to the number of the sons of Israel". The Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j and the Septuagint read "sons of God", which reflects the older idea of a heavenly council and was changed to avoid it.
  • Genesis 2:2. "On the seventh day God finished His work": the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Peshitta read "on the sixth day", avoiding the implication that God worked on the Sabbath.
  • A lost paragraph. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a preserves a paragraph about Nahash the Ammonite before 1 Samuel 11 that dropped out of the Masoretic Text; some modern translations (NRSV) restore it.
  • Two editions. The Septuagint of Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter and arranged differently; scholars recognise it as an earlier edition, with a Hebrew equivalent at Qumran (4QJer-b). Joshua also survives in a different edition.
  • The Masoretic Text of Samuel is "frequently corrupt", and translators often have to emend or bracket unintelligible readings.
  • Gospels quote the Greek. Mark 7:6-7 has Jesus quote Isaiah 29:13, "in vain do they worship me", which is the Septuagint wording, not the Hebrew.

"The Dead Sea Scrolls prove the text is accurate (Isaiah scroll)."

The Great Isaiah Scroll is close to the Masoretic Text, but the Scrolls also show multiple text forms circulating at once (proto-Masoretic, Septuagint-like, Samaritan-like), which is the opposite of a single preserved text.

Your opponent says

“Small variants don't matter; the message is intact.”

Deuteronomy 32:8 changes the theology of God's council, Genesis 2:2 changes what God did on the Sabbath, and Jeremiah exists in two editions of different length. Tov, a Jewish scholar, says most scholars accept that theological changes were made.

Tov accepts deliberate theological changes in the Hebrew Bible: Deuteronomy 32:8 changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel", Genesis 2:2 has competing days, a paragraph of Samuel was lost, and Jeremiah survives in two editions.

s-corruption--the-canon-itself-was-dispu.html: Christians did not agree on which books belonged in the New Testament until the 4th century or later, and leading figures, including Reformers, rejected books that are now canonical.

1. P1If God had preserved His revelation in the Bible, His followers would know which books are revealed.
  2. P2Revelation, Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2-3 John were disputed for centuries; some churches still use different canons; Luther and Zwingli rejected books.
  3. ∴The Bible's contents were decided by human judgement over time, not received as a fixed revelation.

• Eusebius (c. 325) lists Revelation among both "accepted" and "rejected" books and lists James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2-3 John as "disputed" (Church History 3.25).
  • Revelation was omitted by Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechetical Lectures 4.36), Gregory of Nazianzus, the Synod of Laodicea, Chrysostom and Theodoret. Amphilochius said "the majority say it is spurious". Dionysius of Alexandria argued from its Greek style that it was not by the author of John's Gospel. Luther called it "neither apostolic nor prophetic", and Zwingli rejected it.
  • Luther called James "an epistle of straw" and placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his Bible as of lesser rank. Calvin doubted 2 Peter.
  • Jude quotes the Book of Enoch as genuine prophecy (Jude 14-15, quoting 1 Enoch 1:9), and some fathers rejected Jude for that reason. Only the Ethiopian church includes Enoch in its Bible today.
  • Different canons today. Catholics include seven books Protestants reject; the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is commonly counted as 81 books.
  • The Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas are bound into Codex Sinaiticus as part of the Bible.

"The church recognised, not decided, the canon."

Then Luther, Zwingli, Cyril of Jerusalem and the Synod of Laodicea all failed to recognise it, and the Catholic and Protestant churches still recognise different books. Recognition that took centuries and still differs is indistinguishable from decision.

Your opponent says

“The Quran was also compiled after Muhammad's death.”

It was compiled from what he dictated and what the Companions had memorised, within two years, and no Companion disputed the Quran's contents in a way that survived the standardisation; reports about Ibn Mas'ud's codex show the point was discussed and settled. The Bible's canon was disputed for 300 years and still differs between churches.

Eusebius listed books as disputed; Revelation was omitted by major fathers and councils; Luther demoted four books; Jude quotes Enoch; and churches still use different canons. The Bible's contents were settled by human judgement over centuries.

s-corruption--historical-errors-and-misq.html: The Gospels and Acts misattribute Old Testament quotations, cite prophecies that do not exist, and record events that contemporary historians do not know.

1. P1An inspired text should not misquote the Bible it relies on or invent prophecies.
  2. P2Matthew attributes Zechariah to Jeremiah and cites a "Nazarene" prophecy that is not in the OT; Mark names the wrong high priest; Acts confuses two burial plots; Matthew reports a massacre no historian knows.
  3. ∴These texts contain human errors.

• Matthew 27:9 attributes to Jeremiah a prophecy about thirty pieces of silver that is actually from Zechariah 11:12-13.
  • Matthew 2:23: "he shall be called a Nazarene" is not in the Old Testament.
  • Mark 2:26: Jesus says David ate the holy bread "in the time of Abiathar the high priest", but 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Ahimelech. Matthew and Luke both drop the name.
  • Matthew 23:35: "Zechariah the son of Barachiah", murdered between the sanctuary and the altar, was actually the son of Jehoiada (2 Chr 24:20-21).
  • Acts 7:16: Stephen says Abraham bought a tomb at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, but Abraham bought his tomb at Hebron from Ephron (Gen 23), and it was Jacob who bought land at Shechem from Hamor (Gen 33:19).
  • Herod's massacre of the infants (Matt 2:16). Josephus records Herod's crimes in detail, including killing his own sons, but never mentions it. Geza Vermes notes that the star, the Magi, the massacre and the flight to Egypt are found "only in Matthew".
  • Eusebius' "anachronism". Christians mock the Quran for calling Abraham and Moses Muslims, yet Eusebius wrote that the righteous from Abraham back to the first man were "Christians in fact, if not in name" (Church History 1.4), using the word in its meaning of a faith rather than a later label, exactly as the Quran uses muslim.

"Matthew 27:9 combines Jeremiah and Zechariah and names the major prophet."

Matthew's quotation is about thirty pieces of silver paid and thrown to the potter, which is Zechariah's text; Jeremiah's field purchase (Jer 32:6-15) involves seventeen shekels of silver, not thirty, and the potter scene is in Jer 18-19. Scribes themselves found it a problem (some manuscripts change the name).

"Abiathar" means "in the passage about Abiathar".

Ahimelech is the priest in the passage; Abiathar appears only after the massacre in the next chapter. Matthew and Luke both deleted the name, which suggests they saw a problem.

Your opponent says

“Small errors don't affect the message.”

They affect the claim that the text is inspired word for word. And the Gospel writers used these quotations to prove Jesus' messiahship; if the proofs are misquoted or invented, the argument they support fails.

Matthew cites Jeremiah for Zechariah and a non-existent "Nazarene" prophecy; Mark names the wrong priest; Matthew names the wrong Zechariah; Acts confuses two tombs; and Herod's massacre is unknown to Josephus.

s-messianic--isaiah-53-the-suffering-ser.html: Isaiah repeatedly names the servant as Israel; in chapter 53 the speakers are the astonished nations; and the servant is promised offspring and long life, which does not fit a dying divine saviour.

1. P1The identity of "the servant" must be determined from Isaiah's own usage and the context of chapters 52-53.
  2. P2Isaiah names the servant as Israel again and again; 52:15 introduces kings of the nations who are shocked; and the servant's reward is "offspring" and "prolonged days".
  3. ∴Isaiah 53 describes the suffering and vindication of Israel (or its righteous remnant), not the atoning death of God incarnate.

• The servant is named. "But you, Israel, My servant, Jacob whom I have chosen" (41:8); "Jacob My servant, Israel whom I have chosen" (44:1); "you are My servant, O Israel" (44:21; 49:3). The NT applies the servant passage of Isaiah 49:6 to Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:47), so even the NT doesn't treat "servant" as a title for Jesus alone.
  • The speakers. 52:15 says "kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for what they had not been told they see". On this reading, chapter 53's "we" are the nations, astonished to see despised Israel exalted. The same theme appears in 49:7 ("kings shall see and arise… because of the LORD") and 60:14.
  • Plural. 53:8 says "for the transgression of my people, a stroke was to them (lamo)", a plural pronoun.
  • Offspring and long life. "He shall see his offspring (zera); he shall prolong his days" (53:10). Zera elsewhere in the Bible means physical descendants. A God-man who dies childless does not fit.
  • One ancient Jewish reading takes the passage as Israel; others, such as Targum Jonathan and b. Sanhedrin 98b, take it as the Messiah. Origen reports that a Jewish sage told him the passage refers "to the whole people regarded as one individual", in their dispersion and suffering (Contra Celsum 1.55). The Aramaic Targum makes the servant of 52:13 the Messiah, but transfers the suffering in chapter 53 to Israel in exile; the Messiah intercedes and rebuilds the Temple. He does not die.
  • Suffering for others is a national idea. Lamentations 5:7: "Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we bear their iniquities." 4 Maccabees (6:28-29; 17:21-22) says the martyrs' deaths atoned for Israel. None of this needs a divine victim.
  • "Cut off from the land of the living" (53:8) is used of Israel in exile: "our bones are dried up… we are cut off" (Ezek 37:11), before God brings them back to life.

"Israel is sinful, but the servant is innocent (53:9)."

The prophets distinguish the righteous remnant from the nation as a whole, and the passage describes Israel as the nations now see it: suffering unjustly at their hands. And the servant in 42:19 is "blind" and "deaf", which hardly fits a sinless Messiah either.

"Lamo can be singular in poetry."

It occasionally is, but its ordinary meaning is plural, and the plural fits the many explicit identifications of the servant as Israel.

"Jewish scholars only reinterpreted it as Israel after Christianity."

Origen, writing around 248, reports a Jewish interlocutor who read it of the whole people (Contra Celsum 1.55)

Your opponent says

“Isaiah 53 describes the crucifixion so precisely it must be about Jesus.”

Read it with 52:13-15: the servant is "exalted", kings are shocked, and he sees "offspring" and "long days". The precise details Christians see (pierced, silent, buried with the rich) are general or mistranslated. Isaiah itself names the servant as Israel at least eight times.

Isaiah names the servant as Israel repeatedly; chapter 53's "we" are the astonished kings of 52:15; the servant gets offspring and long life; and the Targum keeps the suffering with Israel, not the Messiah.

s-messianic--psalm-22-like-a-lion-not-th.html: The Hebrew of Psalm 22:16 says "like a lion [at] my hands and my feet", matching the animal imagery of the whole psalm. The Gospels quote Psalm 22 repeatedly but never verse 16.

1. P1A prophecy proof needs the text actually to say what is claimed.
  2. P2The Masoretic Hebrew reads ka'ari, "like a lion"; the verb for "pierce" in Hebrew is different; and the Gospel writers, who quote Psalm 22 several times, never cite verse 16.
  3. ∴Psalm 22:16 is not a prophecy of crucifixion.

• The word. The Hebrew is ka'ari, "like the lion", the same word for lion used in verses 13 and 21 ("a ravening and roaring lion"; "save me from the mouth of the lion"). The psalmist is surrounded by "dogs" (v. 16a) and "bulls" (v. 12). The NIV itself notes: "most Hebrew manuscripts: like the lion".
  • "Pierce" in Hebrew is daqar (Zech 12:10), ratsa or naqav. Even the alternative reading karu, which a Judean-desert scroll may support, would mean "dug", not "pierced", according to the standard lexicon (HALOT).
  • The Gospels' silence. The Gospels quote Psalm 22:1 ("My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?"), 22:7-8 (mocking) and 22:18 (dividing the garments). If verse 16 had said "they pierced my hands and feet", it would have been the strongest prophecy of all, yet no Gospel quotes it.
  • Other readings. The Talmud (Megillah 15b) applies Psalm 22 to Esther. The Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns apply Psalms 22 and 118 to the Teacher of Righteousness, saved from his persecutors.
  • The psalm ends in rescue. "He has not despised the affliction of the afflicted… he has heard when he cried to Him" (22:24). The sufferer is saved.

"The Septuagint says 'they dug/pierced'."

The Septuagint has oryxan, "they dug", which still is not "pierced", and comes from a Hebrew text read differently. A sentence "like a lion my hands and feet" is elliptical in Hebrew, which is why translators tried other readings. The surrounding verses fix the image as animals attacking.

Your opponent says

“The Dead Sea Scrolls prove "pierced" is original.”

The relevant scroll (from Nahal Hever) is damaged and debated; even its best-case reading is ka'aru, "they dug" or a variant spelling of "like a lion". It does not say "pierced", and the Gospel writers never used the verse.

Psalm 22:16 in Hebrew says "like a lion", matching the lions, dogs and bulls of the psalm. "Pierce" is a different Hebrew word, the Gospels never quote the verse, and the psalm ends with God rescuing the sufferer.

s-messianic--isaiah-7-14-a-sign-for-king.html: The "young woman" of Isaiah 7:14 was already pregnant, and the sign was to come true within that child's infancy, during the war Ahaz faced in 734-732 BCE.

1. P1A sign given to a king about his immediate crisis must be fulfilled in that crisis.
  2. P2Isaiah offers Ahaz a sign that before the child knows good from evil, the two kings he fears will be gone (7:16), which happened around 732 BCE.
  3. ∴Isaiah 7:14 is about a child born in Isaiah's time, not about Jesus' virgin birth.

• The crisis. Kings Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel were attacking Judah. Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear and offers a sign: "Behold, the young woman (ha-almah) is pregnant and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel… before the boy knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted" (7:14-16). Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BCE, Pekah was killed the same year, and Samaria fell about ten years later (2 Kgs 15:29-30; 16:9).
  • "The young woman". The Hebrew has the definite article and the adjective harah ("pregnant"), usually read as describing a specific woman who is already pregnant. Almah means a young woman of marriageable age (compare "the way of a man with an almah", Prov 30:19; the masculine elem means "young man"). When Isaiah means virgin he uses betulah, as he does five times.
  • The next chapter. Isaiah 8:3-4 describes the birth of a sign-child to Isaiah's wife with the same timetable, and 8:8 addresses "your land, O Immanuel". The sign belongs to Isaiah's own time.
  • Christian scholars agree. Raymond Brown, a Catholic priest, concluded that "the Masoretic Text of Isaiah 7:14 does not refer to a virginal conception in the distant future" (The Birth of the Messiah, pp. 146-149). Already in the 2nd century, the Jew Trypho told Justin it referred to Hezekiah (Dialogue 67).
  • Jesus was not named Immanuel. The angel says "you shall call his name Jesus" (Luke 1:31).

"The Septuagint translates almah as parthenos, 'virgin'."

Parthenos could mean a young woman in general (it is used of Dinah after she was raped, Gen 34:3 LXX). And the Septuagint translators were reading Isaiah's own context, not predicting Jesus.

"Prophecy can have a double fulfilment."

Then the "sign" was already fulfilled in Ahaz's time, and the second fulfilment is a Christian reading, not something the text predicts.

Your opponent says

“Muslims believe in the virgin birth too, so why argue against Isaiah 7:14?”

Muslims believe in the virgin birth because the Quran teaches it (3:47; 19:20), not because of Isaiah 7:14. The point is method: Christians claim the Old Testament predicts their doctrines, and this example shows the claim relies on ignoring context.

Isaiah 7:14 is a sign to King Ahaz that the two kings attacking him would be gone before a child, already conceived, grew up. Almah means young woman, the child is named in Isaiah 8:8, and Raymond Brown agrees it doesn't predict a virgin birth.

s-messianic--zechariah-and-daniel-zerubb.html: Zechariah's king on a donkey is the Davidic governor Zerubbabel; Zechariah 12:10 says the people mourn "to Me" for those killed in a war, and John changed it; and Daniel's seventy weeks start from Cyrus' decree, not a date picked to land on Jesus.

1. P1Prophecies should be read in their historical setting before being applied to later figures.
  2. P2Zechariah's prophecies are set in the rebuilding of the Temple under Zerubbabel; 12:10 is about a war against Jerusalem; and Daniel 9 starts from the decree that ended Jeremiah's seventy years, which points to Cyrus (538 BCE).
  3. ∴These passages refer to figures and events of the prophets' own era and do not predict Jesus' death.

• Zechariah 9:9 ("your king comes to you… riding on a donkey"). Zechariah's hopes centre on Zerubbabel, the Davidic governor who rebuilt the Temple, called "the Branch" (3:8) and God's "signet ring" (Hag 2:23), and in the received text of 6:11-12 the crown is set on Joshua the high priest. Riding a donkey or mule was part of royal coronation (Solomon in 1 Kgs 1:33). Matthew misread the Hebrew parallelism ("on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey") as two animals and has Jesus ride both (Matt 21:7), as Bart Ehrman notes.
