  • Zechariah 12:10 ("they will look on Me, whom they have pierced"). The Hebrew says they will look "to Me concerning (et asher) the one they pierced, and mourn for him". The context is a war in which the nations attack Jerusalem (12:2-9). The Jewish Study Bible translates "they shall lament to Me about those who are slain". John 19:37 quotes it as "they will look on him whom they pierced", changing "Me" to "him".
  • Daniel 9:24-27. The seventy "weeks" (490 years) count from "the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem" (9:25). Daniel is reflecting on Jeremiah's seventy years (9:2), and the decree that ended them was Cyrus', whom Isaiah calls God's "anointed" (mashiach) and says "he shall build My city" (Isa 44:28; 45:1, 13). On the critical reading the 490 years run from Jeremiah's oracle (c. 605/587 BCE) to the Maccabean crisis, ending nowhere near Jesus. Christian calculations choose 457 or 445 BCE and adjust the years to fit. The "anointed one cut off" (9:26) is most likely the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BCE.

"Zerubbabel never became king."

Zechariah's hopes for him were real but went unfulfilled, which is a problem for Zechariah's prediction, not evidence that it was about someone 500 years later.

"Daniel 9 leads exactly to AD 33."

Only by choosing the decree of Artaxerxes and using "prophetic years" of 360 days. Daniel 9:2 ties the prophecy to Jeremiah's seventy years, which ended with Cyrus.

Your opponent says

“The 70 weeks are the most precise prophecy in the Bible: the Messiah must come before the Temple's destruction in 70 AD.”

Daniel calls Cyrus' era "the word to restore Jerusalem" (Isa 44:28 explicitly), and the "anointed one" can be a priest or king (Cyrus himself is called mashiach). Many evangelical scholars, like the JETS article shown, now admit Cyrus' decree is the natural starting point.

Zechariah 9:9 is about Zerubbabel and Matthew turned its parallelism into two animals; Zechariah 12:10 mourns "to Me" for the slain, and John changed it; Daniel 9 counts from Cyrus' decree and doesn't reach Jesus.

s-messianic--genesis-3-15-psalm-2-and-is.html: The "first gospel" of Genesis 3:15 is about humans and snakes; Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm; and the servant of Isaiah 42 does not match Jesus' ministry.

1. P1A messianic reading must fit the passage's own subject and details.
  2. P2Genesis 3:15 is part of a curse on snakes; Psalm 2:7 describes God "begetting" the king at his coronation, as with Israel and Solomon; and Isaiah 42's servant does not cry out, establishes law in the earth and fights idolaters.
  3. ∴None of these passages predicts the Christian Jesus.

• Genesis 3:15 ("he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel"). In context, God curses the serpent to crawl on its belly (3:14) and declares enmity between snakes and human beings. Eve is "the mother of all living" (3:20), so her "seed" is humanity. Claus Westermann shows the "protoevangelium" reading begins with Irenaeus in the late 2nd century.
  • Psalm 2. "You are My son; today I have begotten you" (2:7) is the coronation formula for the Davidic king: "I will be a father to him and he shall be a son to Me" (2 Sam 7:14, of Solomon); "he shall cry to Me, You are my Father… I will make him the firstborn" (Ps 89:26-27). God also "begot" Israel (Deut 32:18). "Kiss the son" (2:12) uses the Aramaic bar in a Hebrew psalm; the Septuagint has "embrace discipline", and the Jewish Publication Society "pay homage in good faith". Kissing was homage to the anointed king (1 Sam 10:1).
  • Isaiah 42. The servant "will not cry out or raise his voice in the street" (42:2), but Jesus "cried out" in the Temple (John 7:37) and overturned tables. He "will not be discouraged until he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his law (torah)" (42:4), but Jesus said he came not to abolish the Law (Matt 5:17), although he also gave "a new commandment" (John 13:34) and was distressed to the point of death (Matt 26:38). He is "a light to the nations" while Jesus said he was sent "only to the lost sheep of Israel" (Matt 15:24). He goes out "like a warrior" against his enemies (42:13) and shames idol-worshippers (42:17), while Jesus preached to monotheist Jews. Muslim scholars apply Isaiah 42 to Muhammad ﷺ, whose people, Kedar (42:11), lived in Arabia (see Muhammad ﷺ in earlier scripture).

"Matthew 12:18-21 applies Isaiah 42 to Jesus."

Matthew quotes 42:1-4 for Jesus' quietness in withdrawing from crowds, but leaves out the rest of the chapter: the warrior, the idol-worshippers, Kedar. Selective quotation is the point at issue.

Your opponent says

“Psalm 2 says "kiss the Son lest he be angry", so the Son is divine.”

The word is Aramaic bar in a Hebrew poem, which is why the Septuagint and the JPS translate it differently. Even with "son", the psalm defines him: "today I have begotten you", the coronation of a king God adopts (2 Sam 7:14).

Genesis 3:15 is a curse on snakes, first read as a gospel by Irenaeus; Psalm 2 is a royal coronation psalm; and Isaiah 42's servant, a warrior who brings law to the nations and shames idolaters, does not fit Jesus.

s-messianic--the-jews-expected-a-messiah.html: The disciples and the crowd did not expect a Messiah who would die, the prophets describe a Messiah who rebuilds Israel and brings peace, and the Bible promises that God would save His anointed, exactly as the Quran says of Jesus.

1. P1If Scripture taught that the Messiah would die for sins, Jesus' own disciples and the crowds who knew the Scriptures would expect it.
  2. P2Peter rebuked the very idea, the disciples "understood none of these things", the crowd said "the Christ remains forever", and the Psalms promise God would save His anointed.
  3. ∴Scripture did not predict a dying Messiah; it predicted one God would rescue, which matches the Quran (4:157-158).

• Peter: "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" (Matt 16:22).
  • The disciples: "they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them" (Luke 18:34).
  • Emmaus: "we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21).
  • The crowd: "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever" (John 12:34).
  • Saving the anointed. "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heaven" (Ps 20:6). Psalm 91, which Satan applies to Jesus (Matt 4:6), though Jesus replies by quoting Deuteronomy 6:16 against that use (Matt 4:7), promises "no evil shall befall you… I will deliver him… with long life I will satisfy him" (91:10, 15-16). Angels rescued Daniel and his friends before death (Dan 3:28; 6:22).
  • Unfinished tasks. The prophets' Messiah reigns in justice and Israel dwells safely (Jer 23:5-6; 33:15), gathers the exiles and rebuilds under one shepherd (Ezek 34:23-28; 37:24-28), and brings peace to the ends of the earth (Mic 5:4). Instead, the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE. Christians reply that these will be fulfilled at the second coming, which concedes they were not fulfilled in Jesus' life.
  • The Quran's account fits. Allah restrained the Children of Israel from Jesus (5:110), raised him (4:158), and he will return, break the cross and establish justice (Bukhari 2476), a time of peace like Isaiah's wolf dwelling with the lamb (Isa 11:6).

وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ

5:110

"Jesus explained the Scriptures about his suffering on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27)."

Luke doesn't say which Scriptures, and the ones Christians usually cite are those examined above, which do not say what is claimed. Luke 24:46 ("thus it is written that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day") quotes no actual text, and the passages Christians usually cite are answered elsewhere.

Your opponent says

“The Jews misunderstood their own prophecies; Jesus corrected them.”

Then God's revelation about the Messiah's central mission was so unclear that the Messiah's closest disciples, after years with him, "understood none of it". Meanwhile the Psalms they did read say God saves His anointed, which is what the Quran says happened.

Peter, the disciples, the Emmaus pair and the crowd all expected a Messiah who would not die. The Psalms promise God would save His anointed, and the prophets' messianic tasks were left unfulfilled. The Quran's Jesus, rescued and returning, fits.

s-messianic--prophecies-that-do-not-exis.html: Several NT passages say "as it is written" or "according to the Scriptures" for statements found nowhere in the Old Testament. Either the NT authors erred, they cited loosely or interpretively, or they relied on scripture that has since been lost.

1. P1A citation formula ("as it is written") claims that the words are in Scripture.
  2. P2Matthew 2:23, Luke 24:46, John 7:38, 1 Corinthians 15:4, 1 Corinthians 2:9 and James 4:5 cite texts that are not in the Old Testament.
  3. ∴Either the NT writers made errors, or scripture was lost, and either conclusion undermines the Christian view of a complete, preserved Bible.

• Matthew 2:23: "He shall be called a Nazarene", said to be "spoken by the prophets". No such verse exists. Geza Vermes notes that Hebrew netser ("branch") and Nazoraios are not even the same root. The Oxford Bible Commentary agrees there is no such text.
  • Luke 24:46: "Thus it is written that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead." No OT text says this.
  • 1 Corinthians 15:4: "raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures". Christians cite Hosea 6:2 ("on the third day he will raise us up"), which is about Israel's restoration and uses "us".
  • John 7:38: "As the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water." No such text.
  • 1 Corinthians 2:9: "As it is written, what no eye has seen…" Only loosely like Isaiah 64:4; Chrysostom suggested it came from lost books. Notably, the same saying appears in a hadith qudsi about Paradise ("what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined", Bukhari 3244).
  • James 4:5: "Do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, 'He yearns jealously over the spirit that He has made to dwell in us'?" No OT source.
  • Matthew 27:9: thirty pieces of silver "spoken by Jeremiah" are in Zechariah 11:12-13; scribes changed the name in some manuscripts (Metzger).
  • Matthew 2:17-18: Rachel weeping for her children (Jer 31:15) is about the Babylonian exile, and the next verses say "they shall come back from the land of the enemy" (31:16), which doesn't fit infants killed in Bethlehem.

"Matthew 2:23 is a wordplay on netser (Isa 11:1)."

Matthew says "spoken by the prophets", plural, and gives a sentence, not a pun. Christian commentators from Adam Clarke to modern apologists admit there is no tidy answer.

"'According to the Scriptures' means the general teaching of Scripture."

Then "it is written" doesn't mean what it says. In James 4:5 and John 7:38 the formula introduces a specific quotation.

Your opponent says

“These are minor; there are hundreds of real prophecies.”

The NT writers present these as proofs. When the proof-texts are missing, misattributed or out of context, the apologetic list shrinks to texts that, as this section shows, are about Israel, Ahaz, Zerubbabel or Cyrus.

"He shall be called a Nazarene", "the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day" and "rivers of living water" are quoted as Scripture but exist nowhere in the OT. Either the NT erred or scripture was lost.

s-pagan--the-gods-have-come-down-in-the-.html: The idea of a god appearing as a man, a son of god born miraculously who works wonders and ascends, was familiar to the Greco-Roman world, and the NT itself shows pagans reading Paul's message that way.

1. P1If a doctrine fits pagan expectations and contradicts Jewish monotheism, it is more likely a product of the pagan environment than of the Jewish prophets.
  2. P2Greco-Roman religion was full of gods in human form and divine sons of gods; pagan crowds identified Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes; the language of Philippians 2:7 resembles Dionysus' self-description in Euripides.
  3. ∴The incarnation fits the pagan world, not the Jewish one Jesus belonged to.

• At Lystra the crowd cried "the gods have come down to us in the likeness of men", called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and a priest of Zeus brought bulls to sacrifice (Acts 14:11-13). At Malta, people said Paul was a god (Acts 28:6).
  • Dionysus opens Euripides' Bacchae: "I have changed my form from god to mortal" and "I have taken the likeness of a man" (lines 4, 53). Philippians 2:7: "taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men".
  • Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century teacher, was said, in Philostratus' Life (written c. 220-240 CE), to have had a miraculous birth announced by a divine being, to have been called a son of God, to have raised the dead and ascended (Philostratus). Bart Ehrman opens How Jesus Became God (pp. 10-15) with him, to show how normal such claims were.
  • Emperors were proclaimed divine: an inscription at Ephesus calls Julius Caesar "god manifest" and "saviour of human life".

وَقَالَتِ النَّصَارَى الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ اللَّهِ ۖ ذَٰلِكَ قَوْلُهُم بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ ۖ يُضَاهِئُونَ قَوْلَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن قَبْلُ

9:30

"Christianity is Jewish; the incarnation came from Jewish categories like Wisdom and the Word."

Jewish personified Wisdom was never worshipped or said to become a man. The only people in the NT who spontaneously recognise gods in human form are the pagans at Lystra.

"Parallels don't prove borrowing."

True, and you should not claim direct copying. The argument is that the idea of a god becoming man was at home in Greek religion, while Jewish scripture has only temporary appearances such as Genesis 18, so the doctrine's growth is best explained by the Gentile environment of the church.

Your opponent says

“Paul tore his clothes at Lystra when they called him a god, so Christianity rejects pagan ideas.”

He rejected being called a god himself. But the belief that God had come in human form is precisely what Christianity then taught of Jesus. The Lystrans' instinct was the same, just applied to different men.

The NT itself shows pagans saying "the gods have come down in the likeness of men"; Dionysus says he took "the likeness of a man"; Apollonius and emperors were called sons of god and saviours. The incarnation fits that world, not the prophets'.

s-pagan--divine-triads-were-common-in-pa.html: A three-fold unity of gods appears in Egyptian religion (Papyrus Leiden I 350), and the Pythagoreans gave sacred significance to the number three, and the Church fathers admitted the Trinity was a middle way between Jewish and Greek belief.

1. P1A theology that matches existing pagan formulas and is described by Gregory of Nyssa as a middle path between Jewish and Greek errors has a non-biblical origin.
  2. P2Egyptian hymns describe Amun, Re and Ptah as three gods who are one; Pythagoreans used triads in worship; and Gregory of Nyssa describes the Trinity as taking something from Jewish and something from Greek belief.
  3. ∴The Trinity has roots in the pagan world rather than the prophetic tradition.

• Egypt. A Leiden hymn to Amun (13th century BCE): "All gods are three: Amun, Re and Ptah, whom none equals. He hides his name as Amun, he appears to the face as Re, his body is Ptah." Jan Assmann (Of God and Gods, p. 64) and Siegfried Morenz discuss it as a Trinitarian formula.
  • Greece. Aristotle reports that the Pythagoreans regarded three as the number of the whole and used the triad in the worship of the gods (On the Heavens 1.1).
  • Gregory of Nyssa (Catechetical Oration 3) presents the doctrine as avoiding both errors: it takes the unity of nature from the Jews and the distinction of persons from the Greeks.
  • G.L. Prestige notes that Tertullian's trinitas meant a triad, not yet a tri-unity.

"Pagan triads are three separate gods, not three persons in one being."

The Leiden hymn explicitly says the three are one god with one hidden name, which is as close as the ancient world gets to the later formula. And Gregory himself says the doctrine takes the distinction of persons from the Greeks, while rejecting their polytheism.

Your opponent says

“Similarity isn't borrowing; you could say Islam copied pagan monotheism (Akhenaten).”

Islam's monotheism is the continuation of Abraham, Moses and the prophets, which Jews and Christians also claim. The Trinity's three-in-one formula has no precedent in the prophets but does in Egypt and Greece, and a Cappadocian father admits it borrows from the Greeks.
An Egyptian hymn says "all gods are three… whom none equals", the Pythagoreans worshipped with triads, and Gregory of Nyssa called the Trinity a middle way between Jewish and Greek belief.

s-pagan--eating-a-god-s-flesh-and-drinki.html: The Torah strictly forbids consuming blood, the Jerusalem apostles kept that rule for Gentiles, and the Ebionites, a later Jewish-Christian group, held a simple remembrance meal. The sacramental Eucharist, with its pagan parallels, is found in Paul, John and the Synoptic Gospels.

1. P1Jesus, a Torah-observant Jew, would not command a ritual that the Torah forbids on pain of being "cut off".
  2. P2The Torah forbids drinking blood on pain of being "cut off" (Lev 17:10-14); the apostles reaffirmed it for Gentiles (Acts 15:20); the Ebionites' meal used water and bread in remembrance; Justin Martyr admits a similar rite existed in the mysteries of Mithras.
  3. ∴The sacramental meal of flesh and blood is a later development foreign to Jesus' Judaism.

• The Law. "If anyone of the house of Israel… eats any blood, I will set My face against that person… for the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:10-11). The Jerusalem council told Gentile believers to abstain "from blood" (Acts 15:20).
  • John 6. When Jesus says "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53), "many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him" (6:66). John's own text shows how foreign the idea was to Jews.
  • Paul is the earliest source for the words of institution (1 Cor 11:23-26), which he says he "received from the Lord" (a phrase scholars read either as tradition or as direct revelation).
  • Mithras. Justin Martyr says "wicked devils have imitated" the Eucharist "in the mysteries of Mithras, commanding the same thing to be done: bread and a cup of water are placed with certain incantations" (1 Apology 66). He explains the similarity by demonic imitation in advance; a historian would note the existing mystery-meal pattern.
  • The Ebionites used unleavened bread and water in a yearly remembrance meal (Irenaeus; Epiphanius; Schoeps, Jewish Christianity, p. 62).

"It's symbolic in many churches."

Catholic and Orthodox doctrine says it becomes the real flesh and blood. Even as a symbol, drinking a person's blood is not a Jewish image; it is the reason the disciples left in John 6.

Your opponent says

“The Last Supper was a Passover meal, which is Jewish.”

Passover is Jewish; "this is my blood, drink it" is not, which is why John reports disciples abandoning Jesus over it and why the Ebionites dropped wine. The Quran's version of the table (5:112-115) is a meal sent down as a sign, with no blood-drinking.

The Torah forbids drinking blood, the apostles reaffirmed it, and disciples left Jesus over "drink my blood" in John 6. Paul is the source of the sacramental formula, Justin admits the Mithras parallel, and the Ebionites used water.

s-pagan--israelite-religion-itself-absor.html: The Hebrew Bible preserves traces of a divine council of gods, a goddess paired with YHWH, and foreign gods with real power. The Quran's monotheism contains none of these, which is what a corrective revelation would look like.

1. P1A pure revelation of God's oneness would not contain polytheistic remnants.
  2. P2The Bible speaks of God judging "among the gods", divides the nations among "the sons of God", records worship of "YHWH and his Asherah", and has a foreign god's "great wrath" drive Israel back.
  3. ∴The biblical text was shaped by Israel's surrounding religion; the Quran restores a monotheism free of these traces.

• The divine council. "God stands in the council of El; in the midst of the gods He holds judgement" (Ps 82:1). "Who is like You among the gods, O LORD?" (Exod 15:11). Jephthah tells the Ammonites, "Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you?" (Judg 11:24).
  • Deuteronomy 32:8-9. In the Dead Sea Scroll and Septuagint, the Most High (Elyon) divided the nations "according to the number of the sons of God", and "the LORD's portion is His people". Scholars such as Mark Smith see here the older idea of El dividing the nations among his sons, with YHWH receiving Israel. On the prevailing scholarly reconstruction, the Masoretic Text changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel".
  • Asherah. Inscriptions at Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom (8th century BCE) bless people "by YHWH and his Asherah" (whether Asherah is a goddess or a cultic symbol is debated). The Bible records an Asherah image in the Temple itself (2 Kgs 21:7; 23:4-7). Thomas Römer (The Invention of God) and Mark Smith describe this as part of ancient Israelite religion. The Quran: "He has taken neither a wife nor a son" (72:3).
  • Chemosh's wrath. In 2 Kings 3, Elisha prophesies that God will hand Moab over to Israel (3:18). When the king of Moab sacrifices his firstborn son on the wall, "there came great wrath upon Israel, and they withdrew" (3:27). Jewish and Christian study Bibles explain it as the wrath of Chemosh, Moab's god, and the Moabite Mesha Stele claims victory. The text records Israel's withdrawal after the king of Moab sacrificed his son.
  • A human-shaped God. God walks in the garden (Gen 3:8), eats with Abraham (Gen 18:8), wrestles with Jacob (Gen 32:24-30), "rests and is refreshed" (Exod 31:17), and appears with "loins" in Ezekiel's vision (Ezek 1:27). The Quran: "There is nothing like Him" (42:11).

وَأَنَّهُ تَعَالَىٰ جَدُّ رَبِّنَا مَا اتَّخَذَ صَاحِبَةً وَلَا وَلَدًا

72:3

لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ ۖ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ

42:11

"The Bible records Israel's sins, it doesn't approve of them."

The Asherah inscriptions are outside the Bible and show popular religion. But Psalm 82, Deuteronomy 32:8 and 2 Kings 3:27 are inside the Bible and present the gods and Chemosh's wrath, though Psalm 82:6-7 pronounces judgement on the gods.

"'Gods' in Psalm 82 are human judges."

Jesus reads it that way (John 10:34), and Muslims can accept that reading. But Deuteronomy 32:8's "sons of God" dividing the nations, and the scribal change to remove it, show the text was being cleaned up later, which is the point.

Your opponent says

“Is Islam then saying the Bible was originally polytheistic?”

No. Islam says the prophets taught pure monotheism, and the text that survives was shaped by the people who transmitted it, including their lapses into the religion around them. The Quran restores the original by removing those traces.

The Bible speaks of God "among the gods", dividing nations among "sons of God" (changed in the Masoretic Text), records an Asherah in the Temple and Chemosh's "great wrath" defeating Israel. The Quran's God has no consort, no council of gods and nothing like Him.

s-pagan--images-and-the-cross-worship-th.html: The Ten Commandments forbid making images for worship. Several early fathers agreed, but later Christianity adopted icons, and Catholic theology even assigns the cross the worship due to God.

1. P1The second commandment forbids making and bowing to images (Exod 20:4-5).
  2. P2Early fathers condemned religious images, but later churches venerated icons, and Aquinas says the cross receives latria, the worship due to God.
  3. ∴Image and cross veneration is a departure from the Law and the early church.

• The commandment. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image… you shall not bow down to them or serve them" (Exod 20:4-5).
  • Early Christians. Clement of Alexandria condemns the making of idols, though he allows simple symbols such as a dove or fish on seal rings (Paedagogus 3.11). Epiphanius of Salamis (late 4th century) tore down a church curtain bearing an image of Christ or a saint as "contrary to the authority of the Scriptures" (Letter 51, preserved by Jerome).
  • Later practice. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) required the veneration of icons. Thomas Aquinas taught that the cross on which Christ died should be given latria, the worship due to God (Summa Theologiae III, q. 25, a. 4).
  • The Quran on Abraham's people: "What are these images to which you are devoted?" (21:52).

"Veneration (dulia) is different from worship (latria)."

Aquinas himself assigns latria to the cross. And the commandment forbids bowing to images, not only "worshipping" in a technical sense.

Your opponent says

“Muslims bow toward the Kaaba, a building.”

Muslims bow to Allah in the direction of the Kaaba; no one prays to it, there is no image, and Umar said of the Black Stone, "I know you are a stone that can neither harm nor benefit" (Bukhari 1597). Aquinas, by contrast, says the cross itself receives the worship due to God.
The second commandment forbids images for worship; Clement and Epiphanius opposed them; but Nicaea II mandated icons and Aquinas assigns the cross latria, the worship due to God.

s-dilemmas--by-their-fruits-satan-does-n.html: Jesus gave the "tree and fruit" test for prophets, and an argument about Satan and exorcism: Satan does not oppose himself, and a tree is known by its fruit. Muhammad ﷺ passes both: he called people away from idols and toward the one God, and his fruit was righteousness. So a Christian must either accept him or reject Jesus' own tests.

1. P1Jesus taught that "if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?" (Matt 12:26) and "every good tree bears good fruit… by their fruits you will recognise them" (Matt 7:17-20).
  2. P2Muhammad ﷺ taught the oneness of God, ended idol worship in Arabia, warned against Satan as "an open enemy" (35:6), and commanded honouring parents, honesty, charity and prayer.
  3. ∴By Jesus' criteria, Muhammad's ﷺ message cannot be from Satan, so Christians must take his prophethood seriously.

The Quran's constant theme is the worship of the God of Abraham alone: "Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him; and to parents do good" (4:36). It says repeatedly that Satan is man's enemy (2:168; 35:6; 36:60). The result was that within one generation Arabia moved from idol worship, infanticide and tribal blood-feuds to monotheism and law.

Non-Muslim historians have said the same about his fruits. W. Montgomery Watt: "to suppose Muhammad an impostor raises more problems than it solves". R. Bosworth Smith said he "ruled by a right Divine". Lamartine asked, measured by the greatness of aim, smallness of means and astounding results, "who could dare compare any great man in modern history with Muhammad?"

Jesus himself was accused of being in league with Beelzebub (Mark 3:22), and gave this answer; Christians who say Muhammad was inspired by Satan repeat the Pharisees' charge.

The Torah adds a second test: a prophet whose prophecies come true (Deut 18:21-22). The Quran's prophecy that Rome would defeat Persia within a few years (30:2-4) was fulfilled; Edward Gibbon wrote that at the time the prediction "is said to have been delivered", "no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment".

إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّ فَاتَّخِذُوهُ عَدُوًّا

35:6

"Satan can appear as an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14), so good teachings could be a trick."

Then the same argument applies to Jesus, and Jesus' test becomes useless. Jesus said Satan does not work against his own kingdom; a message that destroyed idol worship across Arabia and led millions to worship the God of Abraham is working against it.

"Muhammad denied the crucifixion and deity of Christ, which is satanic."

That assumes the conclusion. The test Jesus gave is fruit and opposition to Satan's works, not agreement with later doctrine.

Your opponent says

“Muhammad led wars, so his fruits were bad.”

So did Moses, Joshua and David, whom Christians call prophets. The relevant fruit is what he taught and the society it produced: monotheism, prayer, charity, the protection of orphans and the end of infanticide. That is what Jesus' test looks at.

Jesus said Satan doesn't cast out Satan and a tree is known by its fruit. Muhammad ﷺ ended idol worship, called Satan man's enemy and taught righteousness, and his Rome prophecy came true. By Jesus' own tests, he can't be from Satan.

s-dilemmas--god-died-christian-doctrine-.html: Official Christian doctrine says the person who died on the cross was the divine Son, so "God died". The Bible says God is immortal. And Paul says a mediator implies two parties, but "God is one", and calls the mediator "the man Christ Jesus".

1. P1The Bible says God alone has immortality (1 Tim 6:16) and is "the immortal God" (Rom 1:23).
  2. P2The Catholic Catechism (468) and the Second Council of Constantinople (553) teach that the one who was crucified is the divine Person, "one of the Holy Trinity".
  3. ∴Either God died, which contradicts the Bible, or the one who died was not God, which contradicts the doctrine.

• The council. Constantinople II (553), canon 10: "If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ who was crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity, let him be anathema." The Catechism of the Catholic Church (468) cites it.
  • The Bible. God "alone has immortality" (1 Tim 6:16); He is "immortal, invisible, the only God" (1 Tim 1:17).
  • The mediator. "Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one" (Gal 3:20, about the mediator of the Law). "There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). The mediator is distinguished from the one God and called a man.
  • Even the Catechism concedes (441) that "son of God" as a title of the Messiah-king does not in itself imply more than human.

"Only his human nature died."

A nature doesn't die; persons do. The council says the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity". If that Person did not die, then no divine Person died and the sacrifice was a human one; if he did, God died.

Your opponent says

“You don't understand the hypostatic union.”

I'm quoting your own council: the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity". Either that Person died or he didn't. If he died, God died, against 1 Timothy 6:16. If he didn't, then only a man died, and Christianity's infinite sacrifice disappears.

Constantinople II says the one crucified is "one of the Holy Trinity", so God died; the Bible says God alone is immortal. Paul calls the one mediator "the man Christ Jesus", distinct from the one God.

s-dilemmas--jeconiah-s-curse-and-the-two.html: God cursed King Jeconiah's line so that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne. Matthew traces Jesus' line through Jeconiah; Luke traces a different line through Nathan, not Solomon. Either way the Christian Messiah has a problem.

1. P1God said of Jeconiah: "none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David" (Jer 22:30; compare 36:30 about his father Jehoiakim). The messianic promise runs through Solomon (2 Sam 7:12-14; 1 Chr 22:9-10).
  2. P2Matthew's genealogy runs through Jeconiah (Matt 1:11-12). Luke's runs through Nathan, not Solomon (Luke 3:31).
  3. ∴If Jesus is Joseph's legal heir (Matthew), he inherits the curse; if his line is Luke's, it does not come through Solomon. And if he is virgin-born, neither genealogy, which both go through Joseph, makes him David's physical descendant.

• Jeremiah 22:30: "Write this man down as childless… for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
  • Matthew 1:11-12 includes "Jechoniah" in Jesus' line through Joseph.
  • Luke 3:23-31 runs from Joseph back through Nathan, a different son of David.
  • Whose genealogy is Luke's? Christians now often say Luke gives Mary's line. But the text says "Joseph, the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23), and early Christian writers (Julius Africanus, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 1.7; Augustine; John of Damascus) explained the two lists as both belonging to Joseph. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the "Mary's genealogy" theory became popular only from Annius of Viterbo in the 15th century.
  • Zerubbabel, who appears in both lists, was only a Persian governor (Hag 1:14), not a king, so the curse held for him.

"Haggai 2:23 reverses the curse by making Zerubbabel God's signet ring."

Jeremiah 22:24 used the signet-ring image for Jeconiah's rejection. Haggai's use of it for Zerubbabel promised him authority, but he never sat on David's throne; he governed for Persia. The curse's terms (no descendant on the throne) were not lifted in the text.

Your opponent says

“Jesus is the legal heir through Joseph and the biological heir through Mary, so both lines are covered.”

Luke says "Joseph, son of Heli", and the early church took both lists as Joseph's. And neither list gives Mary's ancestry in the text. So Jesus is either Jeconiah's heir (cursed) or has no stated Davidic blood line through Solomon.

God barred Jeconiah's descendants from David's throne (Jer 22:30). Matthew puts Jeconiah in Jesus' line; Luke uses Nathan instead of Solomon; and both lists run through Joseph, who on Christian belief was not Jesus' father.

s-dilemmas--the-bible-s-own-confirmation.html: Christians argue that the Quran confirms the Bible, so Muslims must accept it (the "Islamic dilemma"). But the NT says "all Scripture is God-breathed" and Paul affirms "everything in the Law and the Prophets", while also misquoting them. The same dilemma hits the NT.

1. P1Paul says he believes "everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets" (Acts 24:14), and 2 Timothy 3:16 (a Pastoral letter, regarded as deutero-Pauline) says all Scripture is God-breathed.
  2. P2Paul cites Psalm 68:18 as "he gave gifts" (Eph 4:8), a reading also found in the Targum and Peshitta, and quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 to say the opposite of its meaning (Gal 3:10). The OT he affirms also exists in variant forms.
  3. ∴Either the NT affirms a text it misquotes, or the confirmation is general, not word-for-word, which is exactly the Muslim position about the Quran's confirmation.

• Psalm 68:18: "You ascended on high… receiving gifts among men." Ephesians 4:8: "When he ascended on high… he gave gifts to men." The change is needed for Paul's point about Christ giving gifts to the church.
  • Deuteronomy 27:26: "Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them." Galatians 3:10: "All who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written…" Paul turns a curse on law-breakers into a curse on law-keepers.
  • Variants. The OT Paul cites survives in Hebrew and Greek versions that differ (see Corruption); the NT authors usually follow the Greek.

"Paul was paraphrasing for application."

Then the NT's "confirmation" of the OT allows interpretation and selection, which is all Muslims claim for the Quran's confirmation of earlier books (see The Quran & the earlier scriptures).

Your opponent says

“The Quran says the Torah and Gospel are from God, so you must accept the Bible.”

The Quran confirms what God revealed to Moses and Jesus, and calls itself the guardian over it (5:48). Paul affirmed "everything in the Law and the Prophets" and still changed Psalm 68:18. If affirmation doesn't mean "every word in your copy", my position is the same as Paul's.

Paul affirms everything in the Law and the Prophets but changes "received gifts" to "gave gifts" and reverses Deuteronomy 27:26. So biblical "confirmation" is general, not word-for-word, which is the Muslim view of the Quran's confirmation.

s-dilemmas--the-prophets-say-sacrifices-.html: Hebrews says Christ's sacrifice ended the sacrificial system. But Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Zechariah say that in the messianic age, after the new covenant, Levitical priests will offer sacrifices forever, and the Messiah-prince himself offers a sin offering for himself.

1. P1If the prophets foretold that sacrifices would continue under the Messiah, Christ's death did not end them.
  2. P2Jeremiah 33:17-18 (after the new covenant of 31:31) promises priests offering sacrifices continually; Ezekiel's prince offers a sin offering "for himself"; Zechariah 14:21 has sacrifices in the final age.
  3. ∴Either Hebrews is wrong, or the Christian Jesus is not the Messiah of the prophets.

• Jeremiah 33:17-18: "David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of Israel, and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in My presence to offer burnt offerings… and to make sacrifices forever." Verse 21 binds the two promises together. This follows the "new covenant" promise of 31:31.
  • Ezekiel 45:22: in the restored Temple, "the prince shall provide for himself and all the people of the land a young bull for a sin offering". Ezekiel 37:24-25 speaks of "David My servant" as prince, which many read as the Messiah, though the prince of chapters 40-48 is not named. A sinless Messiah would not need a sin offering for himself.
  • Zechariah 14:21: in the final age, "all who sacrifice will come and take [the pots] and boil the meat in them".
  • Hebrews 10:11-18: Christ's single offering has ended sacrifice for sin.

"These are symbolic or memorial sacrifices."

Ezekiel 45:22 calls it a sin offering, and the prince offers it for himself. Calling it symbolic is a way of admitting the text does not fit.

Your opponent says

“Hebrews explains that the old sacrifices were shadows of Christ.”

Hebrews says so, but Jeremiah says the Levitical priests will offer sacrifices "forever" after the new covenant, and Ezekiel's messianic prince offers one for himself. Hebrews contradicts the prophets it claims to fulfil.

Jeremiah promises Levitical sacrifices forever after the new covenant; Ezekiel's Davidic prince offers a sin offering for himself; Zechariah has sacrifices in the last age. Hebrews says they ended with Christ.

s-dilemmas--do-whatever-the-pharisees-te.html: Jesus told his followers to obey the scribes and Pharisees "who sit on Moses' seat", who taught the Law, circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. Christians who follow Paul in abandoning these disobey Jesus' explicit command.

1. P1Jesus: "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do" (Matt 23:2-3).
  2. P2The Pharisees taught circumcision, Sabbath, food laws and the oral law, which Paul and later Christianity rejected.
  3. ∴Christianity has followed Paul rather than Jesus on the practice of the Law.

Jesus' criticism in Matthew 23 was of hypocrisy, though he also criticised their traditions (Matt 15:1-9; 16:12). He even says they should tithe mint and dill while not neglecting justice (Matt 23:23). Compare Paul: circumcision makes Christ of no advantage (Gal 5:2), and "let no one pass judgement on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a Sabbath" (Col 2:16).

"This was before the cross; the Law ended afterwards."

Jesus' instructions in Matthew are given as permanent teaching for disciples (Matt 28:20, "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you"). And the Jerusalem church continued to keep the Law after the cross (Acts 21:20).

Your opponent says

“Jesus condemned the Pharisees throughout Matthew 23.”

He condemned their hypocrisy, and in the same breath said "do and observe whatever they tell you". The command is about their teaching from Moses' seat, which included the whole Law.
Jesus said to obey whatever the Pharisees taught from Moses' seat, condemning only their hypocrisy. Paul told believers to ignore food, festival and Sabbath laws. Christians must choose.

s-xn-morality--god-forgives-without-bloo.html: The Old Testament says God forgives the repentant without sacrifice and that a son does not bear his father's sin. The doctrines of original sin and the necessity of blood atonement contradict this.

1. P1If God forgives the repentant directly and holds each person responsible for his own sin, then neither an inherited guilt nor a blood sacrifice is required for salvation.
  2. P2The prophets say that God desires repentance above sacrifice; the wicked man who turns is forgiven; "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father".
  3. ∴Original sin and the need for the cross are not biblical requirements; the Quran's teaching (6:164; 39:53) matches the prophets.

• Personal responsibility. "The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son" (Ezek 18:20). "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children" (Deut 24:16). The Quran: "No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (6:164).
  • Repentance is enough. "If a wicked person turns away from all his sins… he shall surely live; none of the transgressions he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezek 18:21-22). "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (18:23).
  • Not sacrifice. "You will not delight in sacrifice… the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" (Ps 51:16-17). "I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6), which Jesus himself quotes (Matt 9:13). "With what shall I come before the LORD… with burnt offerings?… He has told you what is good: to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God" (Mic 6:6-8). "By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for" (Prov 16:6).
  • Nineveh. The pagan city repented with fasting and sackcloth, and "God relented of the disaster" (Jonah 3:10). No sacrifice, no blood.
  • Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar to "break off your sins by practising righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed" (Dan 4:27).

وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ

6:164

قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِن رَّحْمَةِ اللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا

39:53

"Hebrews 9:22: without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness."

Hebrews says so, but the prophets say the opposite repeatedly, and Leviticus itself allows flour as a sin offering for the poor (Lev 5:11-13). Jonah 3:10 shows a whole city forgiven without blood.

"God's justice requires a penalty to be paid."

Punishing an innocent person for the guilty is the opposite of justice by the Bible's own law (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20). A judge who lets the guilty go and executes an innocent volunteer is not just.

Your opponent says

“If God just forgives, He isn't just. Someone has to pay.”

Ezekiel 18 says God forgives the repentant and "none of his transgressions shall be remembered". Forgiveness means not exacting the debt. If God must punish someone, then He never forgives; He only transfers the punishment, and to an innocent person, which Ezekiel 18:20 forbids.

Ezekiel 18 says the son doesn't bear the father's sin and the repentant are forgiven; the Psalms, Hosea and Micah say God wants a contrite heart, not sacrifice; and Nineveh was forgiven with no blood. Original sin and blood atonement contradict the prophets.

s-xn-morality--war-the-bible-commands-ki.html: Critics call Islam violent, yet the Bible commands the destruction of whole populations, including infants, while Islamic law forbids killing women, children, the old and monks, and requires proportionality.

1. P1A critic must apply the same moral standard to his own scripture.
  2. P2The Bible commands killing infants (1 Sam 15:3), killing boys and non-virgin women while keeping virgin girls (Num 31:17-18), and leaving nothing alive (Deut 20:16). Islamic law forbids deliberately killing non-combatants and commands proportion and peace when the enemy inclines to it.
  3. ∴On the ethics of war, the Quran and Sunnah are stricter than the Bible.

The Bible.

Islam.

"If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant it to him… then deliver him to his place of safety" (9:6). "If you punish, punish with the like of what you were made to suffer" (16:126).

8:61

"Those were specific historical commands, not permanent law; the Quran's commands are permanent."

9:5 is about specific Arab polytheist tribes who broke treaties (9:4, 9:7-13), and the very next verse (9:6) commands granting protection to any who ask and escorting them to safety. Islamic law never permitted killing non-combatants. 1 Samuel 15:3 explicitly orders killing infants.

s-xn-morality--marriage-women-and-modest.html: The Bible's prophets practised polygyny without rebuke, Church law permitted marriage at twelve, and the fathers required women to veil their heads and even their faces. Critics who attack Islam on these points condemn their own tradition.

1. P1If a practice was accepted by the biblical prophets and the Church fathers, Christians cannot treat it as inherently immoral when Islam permits it.
  2. P2Polygyny was practised by Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon, regulated by the Law, allowed in the OT according to Tertullian (who forbade it to Christians), and not forbidden by Scripture according to Luther. The fathers required the veil. Canon law set marriage at twelve for girls.
  3. ∴Christian objections on these points are double standards.

• Polygyny. "If a man has two wives…" (Deut 21:15) regulates it. God says to David, "I gave you your master's wives into your arms" (2 Sam 12:8), and David "did what was right… except in the matter of Uriah" (1 Kgs 15:5). Tertullian says it was lawful for the patriarchs (To His Wife 1.2). Luther wrote in 1524 that he could not forbid a man to marry several wives because it does not contradict Scripture. Biblical scholar Dan McClellan: "the standard in the Bible is polygamy… nowhere identified as sinful." The Quran limits it to four with the condition of justice (4:3), and al-Shafi'i recommended limiting oneself to one.
  • The veil. Paul: "every wife who prays with her head uncovered dishonours her head… if a wife will not cover her head, let her cut her hair short" (1 Cor 11:5-6). Clement of Alexandria: a woman should go out "with her head veiled and her face covered" (Paedagogus 3.11). The Apostolic Tradition (18.5) requires women to cover their heads with an opaque cloth. Tertullian wrote a whole treatise On the Veiling of Virgins.
  • Age of marriage. The Protevangelium of James (2nd century) says Mary was entrusted to an elderly Joseph at twelve. Medieval canon law set the minimum age of marriage at twelve for girls and fourteen for boys, with betrothal from seven. Augustine's fiancée was about two years under the age of marriage when he was in his early thirties (Confessions 6.13).
  • Women's testimony. In Luke 24:11 the apostles dismiss the women's report as "an idle tale". Josephus says that women's testimony was not admitted "on account of the levity and boldness of their sex" (Antiquities 4.219). Jesus told his followers to obey the Pharisees' teaching (Matt 23:2-3).
  • The fathers on women. Tertullian called woman "the devil's gateway" (On the Apparel of Women 1.1).

"The New Testament moved beyond polygamy."

No NT verse explicitly forbids it for ordinary believers; 1 Timothy 3:2 limits overseers to one wife, which implies others had more. And Luther, reading the same NT, could not forbid it.

Your opponent says

“Islam oppresses women with the hijab.”

Paul commands head covering, Clement says face covered, and nuns and Orthodox women still veil. Mary is always shown veiled. The Quran's modesty rule (24:31) is the same tradition, applied to all believing women.

Abraham, Jacob, David and Solomon had several wives, and Luther couldn't forbid it; Paul and Clement required the veil; canon law allowed girls to marry at twelve. Critics who attack Islam on these points condemn their own tradition.

s-xn-morality--the-church-s-own-moral-re.html: Indulgences sold for money, heretics executed by Church teaching, unbaptised infants consigned to hell, the Crusades and the Inquisition: the Church's moral record does not entitle critics to treat Christianity as morally superior.

1. P1If Christians judge Islam by the conduct of Muslims, the same test applies to Christianity.
  2. P2The Church sold remission of punishment for money, taught that heretics deserve death, taught that unbaptised infants are damned (Augustine) and left to a limbo theory, and launched wars that killed millions, including Christians and Jews.
  3. ∴Judged by the conduct of its institutions, Christianity has no moral advantage.

• Indulgences. Pope Leo X authorised indulgences to fund St Peter's Basilica; the preacher Johann Tetzel was associated with the slogan "as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs". Luther's 95 Theses (1517) attacked this. The Catholic Encyclopedia admits the abuses, which continued until the Council of Trent.
  • Infants in hell. Augustine taught that unbaptised infants are damned and that promising them heaven is heresy (On the Soul and its Origin 1.9-11).
  • Heretics. Thomas Aquinas taught that heretics, after a second warning, may be handed to the secular power "to be exterminated from the world by death" (Summa II-II, q. 11, a. 3). Emperor Theodosius' edict of 380 made Nicene Christianity compulsory.
  • The Crusades included the massacres of Rhineland Jews (1096), the slaughter in Jerusalem (1099), and the sack of Christian Constantinople (1204).
  • Prostitution. Augustine wrote, "remove prostitutes from society and you will disturb everything with lust" (On Order 2.4.12), and some medieval bishops (e.g. the Bishop of Winchester) drew income from brothels.

"These are people's sins, not Christianity's teaching."

Indulgence sales were papal policy, and infant damnation and the death of heretics were taught by Augustine and Aquinas, though Aquinas' view was also condemned in effect by Exsurge Domine (1520)

Your opponent says

“Islam spread by the sword.”

Islam spread by conquest in some regions and by trade and preaching in others (Indonesia, West Africa); the Quran says "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and Christian communities survived under Muslim rule for 1,400 years. Christianity was imposed by imperial edicts in 380 and by the Inquisition.

Popes sold indulgences, Augustine damned unbaptised infants, Aquinas taught heretics should be killed, and the Crusades massacred Jews and sacked Constantinople. The Church is in no position to judge Islam by its followers' conduct.

s-xn-morality--allah-does-not-love-the-d.html: Christians contrast "God is love" with Quranic verses saying Allah does not love the wrongdoers. The Bible says God hates evildoers, hated Esau, and makes His love conditional on obedience.

1. P1If the Bible says God hates the wicked and loves conditionally, Christians cannot object to the Quran saying the same.
  2. P2The Bible also says, alongside such verses and in both Testaments, that God loves sinners (John 3:16; Rom 5:8).
  3. ∴The contrast is false.

• "You hate all evildoers" (Ps 5:5); "His soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence" (Ps 11:5).
  • "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" (Mal 1:2-3), repeated by Paul (Rom 9:13).
  • "Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of My house; I will love them no more" (Hos 9:15).
  • "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father" (John 14:21). "Because you listen to these rules and keep them… He will love you" (Deut 7:12-13).
  • The Quran also says Allah loves the doers of good, the repentant, the just and the patient (2:195, 2:222, 5:42, 3:146), and His mercy encompasses everything (7:156).

وَرَحْمَتِي وَسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ

7:156

"'Hate' in Malachi means 'love less'."

Then the Quran's "does not love" can be read the same way, as the withholding of special favour, not malice. The standard has to be applied equally.

Your opponent says

“The Christian God loved the world so much he died for it; the Muslim God loves only the obedient.”

The Bible's God "hates all evildoers" (Ps 5:5) and loves those who keep His commandments (John 14:21). The Quran says Allah's mercy encompasses everything (7:156) and He forgives all sins of those who repent (39:53).

The Bible says God hates evildoers (Ps 5:5; 11:5), hated Esau (Mal 1:3; Rom 9:13), and loves those who keep His commandments (John 14:21). The Quran's "Allah does not love the wrongdoers" says the same.

s-xn-morality--use-with-care-the-embarra.html: When a critic mocks a hadith as disgusting or bizarre, there is almost always a biblical passage at least as striking. Use these only as a mirror, never as mockery of the earlier prophets.
This is purely a tu quoque tool. Muslims believe in the prophets named here and must not mock them; the point is that the critic's standard condemns his own book.

• "The Prophet ﷺ was bewitched / Gabriel squeezed him." Saul, whom the Bible counts among the prophets (1 Sam 10:11), was tormented by "an evil spirit from the LORD" (1 Sam 16:14); Josephus says it choked and suffocated him (Antiquities 6.8.2).
  • "Camel urine is disgusting." God tells Ezekiel to bake bread on human dung, then allows cow dung instead (Ezek 4:12-15).
  • "Hadith about relics and blessings." Elisha's bones raised a dead man (2 Kgs 13:21); power went out of Jesus' garment (Luke 8:46).
  • Violent stories. Elisha's curse brings bears that maul 42 boys for mocking his baldness (2 Kgs 2:23-24); Jephthah sacrifices his daughter (Judg 11); a Levite throws his concubine to a mob (Judg 19:25); David pays for Michal with 200 Philistine foreskins (1 Sam 18:25-27).
  • "Statutes that were not good." God says He gave Israel "statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not live", making them offer their firstborn (Ezek 20:25-26).
  • Cosmology. The earth on pillars (1 Sam 2:8; Job 9:6) and a tree visible "to the end of the whole earth" (Dan 4:11).

Your opponent says

“Your hadith say the Prophet was bewitched. How can a prophet be affected by magic?”

The magic affected his body temporarily, not his revelation, and the Quran's last two surahs were the cure. The Bible says an evil spirit "from the LORD" tormented Saul, a prophet; if that doesn't disqualify the Bible, the hadith doesn't disqualify the Prophet ﷺ.
Saul's evil spirit from the LORD, Ezekiel's dung-baked bread, Elisha's bones and bears, and "statutes that were not good" show that critics who mock hadith would have to mock their own Bible.

s-xn-miracles--what-a-miracle-can-and-ca.html: A miracle is evidence for a prophet only when it accompanies a claim to prophethood and a message. Apparitions and wonders without a claimant or message prove nothing, every religion reports them, and the Bible itself warns that deceptive signs occur.

1. P1A sign authenticates a message only if someone claims to bring the message and points to the sign as proof (as Moses did before Pharaoh).
  2. P2Modern Christian wonders (Zeitoun 1968, Fatima 1917, bleeding hosts) have no prophet claiming a new revelation (Fatima had messages, but none that claimed to supersede the Gospel); similar wonders are reported in Hinduism and other religions; and the Bible says Satan "disguises himself as an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14) and that false prophets show signs (Deut 13:1-3; Matt 24:24).
  3. ∴Such wonders cannot establish Christianity over Islam or any other religion.

• The criterion. In the Quran and the Bible, signs come with prophets as proof of their message (Exod 4:1-9; Quran 7:106-108). An unexplained light or image with no message is not a credential for anyone.
  • Apparitions. Witness accounts of the Fatima "miracle of the sun" (1917) contradict each other; Kevin McClure's study documents the inconsistencies. The Zeitoun lights (1968) carried no message.
  • Other religions. In 1995 statues of Ganesha across India were reported to "drink milk"; scientists explained it by capillary action. If such events prove a religion, they prove Hinduism too.
  • Eucharistic miracles. Catholic sites report consecrated hosts bleeding "type AB blood". Kelly Kearse, a Catholic immunologist, has written that bacteria can share surface antigens with blood types, so AB typing does not show a human source.
  • Relics. In the Middle Ages several churches claimed to hold Jesus' foreskin (the "Holy Prepuce"); Marc Shell documents the competition. A relic economy is not evidence of truth.
  • The Bible's warning. "False christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect" (Matt 24:24).

"Muslims also report miracles of saints."

Islam does not base its truth on them. The Quran rests its case on the Quran itself, the Prophet's ﷺ fulfilled prophecies and his character, which are public and checkable. Karamat of saints are not proof of Islam.

Your opponent says

“Millions saw the sun dance at Fatima. How do you explain that?”

The accounts conflict, people at other locations saw nothing, and staring at the sun produces visual effects. But even granting something happened, it came with no prophet and no new revelation. The Bible itself says deceptive signs will appear (Matt 24:24; 2 Cor 11:14).
Miracles authenticate a prophet's message; Fatima, Zeitoun and bleeding hosts have no prophet, other religions report equivalent wonders, and the Bible warns of deceptive signs. They prove nothing.

s-xn-miracles--christmas-and-the-papacy-.html: Two of the most visible features of Christianity, the feast of Christmas and the authority of the Pope, are absent from the NT and the earliest church.

1. P1If a practice or office was instituted by Jesus or the apostles, it should appear in the NT or the earliest Christian writings.
  2. P2No NT text mentions celebrating Jesus' birth, and the earliest bishops (Clement of Rome, Ignatius) know nothing of a universal Roman authority.
  3. ∴Both developed later and are traditions, not apostolic revelation.

• Christmas. The NT never mentions a feast of Jesus' birth or its date. The sermons in Acts focus on the resurrection; Paul never mentions a birth festival. The 25 December date is first attested in the 4th century.
  • The papacy. 1 Clement (c. 96), written from Rome to Corinth, speaks for "the church of God in Rome", not for a single bishop with universal jurisdiction. Ignatius of Antioch writes to six churches emphasising their bishop, but his letter to Rome mentions no bishop at all and describes the Roman church as the one that "presides in the region of the Romans".

"Matthew 16:18 makes Peter the rock and founds the papacy."

It mentions Peter, not Rome or successors. Eastern Orthodox and Protestant churches read it differently, and the earliest sources show no universal Roman jurisdiction.

Your opponent says

“Muslims celebrate the Prophet's birthday too.”

Many Muslim scholars reject the Mawlid as an innovation precisely because it has no basis in the Quran or Sunnah. Islam distinguishes revelation from later custom; the point is that Christianity has no such check.
The NT never mentions Christmas, and 25 December appears in the 4th century. Clement of Rome writes for a church, not a pope, and Ignatius' letter to Rome mentions no bishop.
